2026-11-06 Friday 12 stories

What Talent Needs to Know 6 opportunities · 6 challenges
Opportunities
  • The Duffers left Netflix for Paramount and still produce every Stranger Things spinoff because the franchise was carved out of their exclusivity, and that carve-out decides who keeps earning from the hit when a creator changes studios. (Project Economics)
  • Fable is selling a format where the performer supplies a face and a voice and the AI builds the rest, so the likeness license itself, how long it runs and where else it can be used, is the deal. (New Revenue Stream)
  • Foreign distributors who used to pay a minimum guarantee for one territory now want a stake in the IP and its merchandise, so a producer bringing an independent animated film to Lokia is negotiating who owns the consumer-products upside along with the presale price. (Rights Ownership)
  • Cramer built his paid club inside CNBC because the network's airtime does the marketing for him, and on-air talent with a loyal audience can now ask a network to build a subscription product around them and share in it. (New Revenue Stream)
  • With most film slots going to franchises and 3 Arts heading to full Lionsgate ownership, original filmmakers need a disciplined budget to get a slot, and 3 Arts clients should ask how conflicts are handled when their manager's owner is also the buyer. (Project Economics)
  • HBO is still a third bidder on high-end drama, and the first new package it buys outright under Skydance will show whether that budget holds, since the run of announcements so far was business closed before the merger.
Challenges & Headwinds
  • Fox now controls Tubi, the Roku Channel and the home screen in more than 100 million households, so a producer licensing a library to free ad-supported streaming has fewer separate buyers and one owner deciding what gets placed in front of viewers.
  • Studios are now pricing effects work on what AI saves, which makes approval over AI-generated shots one of the few places a director still controls how those savings change the picture.
  • Casting choices and release dates now carry a cash price before they are announced, so everyone on a production with advance knowledge, the talent's own team included, is part of a leak risk studios are now policing.
  • California scored the spinoff on the jobs it would add and gave no weight to two decades of Shondaland shows in Los Angeles, so Marinis, who also runs Grey's, runs two series in two states because of a credit decision she did not control.
  • Dumont got a 25-year-old script made by generating every performance himself, so an established director with a stalled project now has a way to finish it without a financier, and the actors who would have been cast are simply not in the budget.
  • Netflix is deciding whether to own a major Los Angeles lot at the same time it cancels leased stage space and shoots where subsidies are richer, so how much Netflix production stays in Los Angeles is still open.
The Duffers' Paramount Deal Carved Out Stranger Things, So Netflix Still Gets the Prequel
Netflix ordered Other Worlds, a 1950s Stranger Things prequel run by Kate Trefry, and the Duffer Brothers produce it from inside an exclusive Paramount overall deal that excludes Stranger Things.
Netflix greenlit Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure, a live-action prequel set in 1955 Nevada, for a 2028 premiere. Kate Trefry, who wrote the Tony-winning stage play The First Shadow, is creator and showrunner. Matt and Ross Duffer co-created it and executive produce but cannot run it day to day because they are under an exclusive overall deal at Paramount; their services on Stranger Things projects through Upside Down Pictures are carved out of that deal. Shawn Levy, now under an overall deal at Disney's 20th Television, also produces through 21 Laps.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): The Duffers left Netflix for Paramount and still produce every Stranger Things spinoff because the franchise was carved out of their exclusivity, and that carve-out decides who keeps earning from the hit when a creator changes studios.
The Facts
  • Title: Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure; live-action prequel; set April 19, 1955, Marion, Nevada; premieres 2028 on Netflix.
  • Creators: Kate Trefry and Matt and Ross Duffer. Trefry is writer and showrunner, her first series as creator. She joined Stranger Things as a staff writer in Season 2 and wrote The First Shadow from a story by her, the Duffers and Jack Thorne.
  • Duffers: under an exclusive overall deal at Paramount. Deadline: "Their executive services on any Stranger Things projects via their Upside Down Pictures are carved out of the pact."
  • Shawn Levy: left Netflix for an overall deal at Disney's 20th Television; executive produces through 21 Laps; not directing.
  • Joe Wright directs episodes 1 to 3 and executive produces. Other EPs: Paul Dichter, Shelley Meals, Andrea Sperling, Pavlina Hatoupis.
  • Stranger Things debuted in 2016 and was Netflix's first owned hit series, with more than 1.2 billion views across Seasons 1 to 4 (Deadline).
  • Second Stranger Things TV spinoff, third overall with The First Shadow. The animated Tales From '85 has two seasons and awaits a renewal decision.
  • Jinny Howe, Netflix Head of Scripted Series, US and Canada: "We're proud to keep building this world with the Duffers, Kate, Shawn Levy, and Joe Wright."

Fox Now Owns Roku, the Front Door to Netflix, YouTube and Disney+ in 100 Million Homes
Fox closed its $22 billion Roku purchase Friday, ahead of the expected 2027 date, and put Roku, Tubi and Fox One in one new division that targets about $400 million in cost savings.
Fox Corp. closed its acquisition of Roku, valued at $22 billion ($160 a share, about $14.2 billion in cash and the rest in Fox Class A stock), well before the expected 2027 timing. Roku founder Anthony Wood joins the Fox board and co-chairs a new Fox Digital Platforms division with Paul Cheesbrough, covering Roku, Tubi, Fox One and Red Seat Ventures. Fox pledged to keep Roku an open platform that does not favor Fox News or Fox One. Roku had $4.1 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, 49 percent from advertising and 40 percent from subscriptions.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Fox now controls Tubi, the Roku Channel and the home screen in more than 100 million households, so a producer licensing a library to free ad-supported streaming has fewer separate buyers and one owner deciding what gets placed in front of viewers.
The Facts
  • Deal: Fox Corp. acquires Roku; valued at $22 billion; $160 a share; about $14.2 billion cash, remainder in Fox Class A common stock. Announced June 2026; shareholders of both companies approved October 14; closed November 6, ahead of the expected 2027 date.
  • Structure: Anthony Wood (Roku founder and CEO) joins the Fox board and is co-chair of Fox Digital Platforms; Paul Cheesbrough is co-chair and CEO of the division. Division includes Roku, Tubi, Fox One, Red Seat Ventures.
  • Fox pledge: preserve Roku "as a leading open ecosystem for the broader streaming industry" (Variety: no automatic advantageous positioning for Fox News or Fox One).
  • Roku: customer base of more than 100 million households. First nine months of 2026 revenue $4.1 billion, up 23 percent; about 49 percent advertising, 40 percent subscriptions. Q3 gross profit $649 million, up 24 percent; Q3 net income $183 million.
  • Synergies: about $400 million of annualized cost savings within two years; Fox expects the deal to add to free cash flow per share by the second full year.
  • Lachlan Murdoch: "The closing of this acquisition advances the long-term strategy of Fox."
  • Context (Puck, Matthew Belloni, 11/6): the deal had been pending at the Justice Department as of his column the same day.

Studios Now Tell VFX Houses to Bring an AI Plan or Not Bid
Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah said studio legal departments barred generative AI early last year, and since this year's third quarter clients have told vendors, "If you don't have an AI strategy, don't bother."
Weta FX, the effects house behind Avatar and The Lord of the Rings, signed a partnership with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency and has worked with Taiwan's Moonshine Studio on generative AI for about six months. Seah said his clients, mainly the four biggest studios and the streamers, moved from a ban to allowing AI with pre-approval by mid-2025 to asking for an AI strategy, mostly to learn how much money it saves. Chief technology officer Kimball Thurston said Weta uses ByteDance's Seedance and Kling where clients permit, hosted outside China. Seah said Weta does not plan to replace artists.
Potential Talent Implication: Studios are now pricing effects work on what AI saves, which makes approval over AI-generated shots one of the few places a director still controls how those savings change the picture.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Daniel Seah, CEO, Weta FX; press briefing in Taipei after a partnership with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) at Taiwan Creative Content Fest.
  • Client sequence (Seah): early 2025, memos from studio legal departments barring generative AI on their work; mid-2025, several clients allowed it with pre-approval and a small number of approved companies; around the turn of the year, clients asked about Weta's AI strategy, mostly for savings; since Q3 2026: "If you don't have an AI strategy, don't bother to work with us."
  • Moonshine Studio (Taiwan animation and VFX): Weta has worked with it for about six months. Screen International headline (body not read): Weta FX will build an AI hub in Taiwan and buy into Moonshine Studio.
  • Tools: Weta builds its own models; uses Kling AI and ByteDance's Seedance where clients permit, hosted outside China (Thurston: "You kind of have to").
  • TAICCA chair Sue Wang called it the biggest deal Taiwan has struck in the content industry. Taiwan's Ministry of Culture will introduce young talent to Weta; possible internships in Wellington, Melbourne, Vancouver.
  • Weta runs an open-source project, the Rongotai Model Train Club, that writes model training and dataset use into image metadata.
  • Thurston: "People still want to see the big star performing."

Grimes Lent Her Likeness and Voice to an AI Film Opening in Theaters December 4
AI studio Fable cast Grimes's likeness and spoken performance in an AI-generated sci-fi anthology directed by Jack London, known online as Gossip Goblin, and bills it as the first AI film in theaters.
Fable, an AI studio, is releasing an AI-generated sci-fi anthology on December 4 and calls it the first AI film to come to theaters. Grimes appears through her likeness and her own vocal performance. In a press release Fable said casting an actor's likeness with their spoken performance will become more common in AI animated films, with actors, athletes and musicians appearing that way. The Verge did not report a distributor, a theater count or Grimes's terms.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Fable is selling a format where the performer supplies a face and a voice and the AI builds the rest, so the likeness license itself, how long it runs and where else it can be used, is the deal.
The Facts
  • Film: Gods Don't Give Gifts, AI-generated sci-fi anthology; release date December 4, 2026; billed by Fable as "the first AI film to come to theatres."
  • Producer: Fable (AI studio). Director: Jack London, known online as Gossip Goblin.
  • Grimes contributes her likeness and vocal performance.
  • Fable press release: "casting the likeness of an actor with their spoken vocal performance will become more common with animated films using AI: audiences will see actors, athletes, musicians giving vocal performances with their likeness in films."
  • Premise: four interconnected stories set in a future "where bodies are disposable and consciousness has been commoditized."
  • Not reported: distributor, theater count, Grimes's compensation or license terms.

Twelve Foreign Distributors Pooled Into Lokia to Own the IP, Not Just Buy Territories
Distributors including Wild Bunch Germany, Kazoo Films and Noori Pictures formed Lokia, a Luxembourg company that will develop, finance and license films together as international presales decline.
Distributors from 12 territories formed Lokia ahead of the American Film Market, Deadline reported. Partners keep buying separately for their own markets but plan to develop and produce together, share revenue forecasts, invest in the IP and later acquire as a group. Founder Michael Favelle of Odin's Eye said licensing campaigns for independent animated films are not realistic without worldwide theatrical guarantees before financing. Former Marvel licensing executive Russell Brown is in talks with toy, game and publishing partners, with announcements expected in the fourth quarter. Fintage House will manage collection accounts.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Foreign distributors who used to pay a minimum guarantee for one territory now want a stake in the IP and its merchandise, so a producer bringing an independent animated film to Lokia is negotiating who owns the consumer-products upside along with the presale price.
The Facts
  • Lokia: incorporated in Luxembourg; distribution network of buyers from 12 territories, announced November 6, 2026, before AFM.
  • Partners: Wild Bunch Germany and Wild Bunch Austria; Praesens-Film (Switzerland); PRIS Audiovisuals (Portugal); Feelgood Entertainment (Greece); Kazoo Films (UK and Ireland); Noori Pictures (South Korea, Thailand, Vietnam); Filmhouse (Israel); Blitz Group (former Yugoslavia); Donart Film (Czech Republic); Mars Production (Turkey); Horizon Distribution (global airlines and shipping).
  • Plan: develop and produce together, pool market intelligence, pursue licensing and merchandising, later acquire as one entity; partners remain standalone financial entities and keep acquiring individually.
  • Deadline: "a direct response to consolidation in the market and the challenge posed by the declining international pre-sales model."
  • Principals: Michael Favelle (Odin's Eye Entertainment, chief creative officer and president of distribution); Heiko Nemmert (formerly Baby Giant, COO and president of production); Russell Brown (former Marvel Enterprises EVP of worldwide licensing, chief capital and monetisation officer).
  • Lokia OS: partners submit projects, distributors return revenue forecasts, financing and licensing partners see the aggregated picture before capital is committed.
  • Fintage House oversees reporting and collection accounts; co-chairman Robbert Aarts joins the board. Licensing partner announcements expected Q4 2026.
  • Prior groupings cited: Vuelta (2023); foreign distributors financing MadRiver films (2024); producers alliance The Creatives.

Jim Cramer Stayed at CNBC and Is Building a Paid Tier on Its Airtime
CNBC will launch a premium tier of Jim Cramer's Investing Club in 2027, with live shows and workshops and a new general manager, under a new long-term contract with Cramer.
Jim Cramer signed a new long-term contract with Versant's CNBC that expands his Investing Club, offered since 2022, with a premium tier in 2027; pricing has not been announced. Cramer told Variety that going independent would lack CNBC's infrastructure and force him to spend his time marketing. CNBC uses its programming to send viewers to the club. Versant wants half its revenue from digital and direct-to-consumer businesses; last quarter its traditional advertising fell 5.3 percent, distribution fees fell 5.8 percent and non-TV revenue rose 9.6 percent.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Cramer built his paid club inside CNBC because the network's airtime does the marketing for him, and on-air talent with a loyal audience can now ask a network to build a subscription product around them and share in it.
The Facts
  • Contract: new long-term deal between Jim Cramer and CNBC (Versant); terms not reported.
  • Investing Club: offered since 2022; access to trades for Cramer's Charitable Trust, stock analysis, videos, daily market analysis, monthly virtual meetings. Premium tier launches 2027 with live shows and workshops; CNBC will hire a general manager; pricing later.
  • Cramer: going alone "would lack the infrastructure"; "When you do it on your own, you have to start over. You have to tell people where you are."
  • KC Sullivan, CNBC president: "It's about super-serving super-passionate audiences." CNBC plans a separate digital subscription for retail investors in early 2027.
  • Peers cited: Sky News "Defence Insider" app at £14.99 a month; MS NOW "Membership" with Rachel Maddow, Nicolle Wallace, Morning Joe.
  • Versant (CEO Mark Lazarus): goal of half of revenue from digital and direct-to-consumer. Last quarter: traditional advertising down 5.3 percent, distribution fees down 5.8 percent, non-TV revenue up 9.6 percent.

Studios Are Banning Employees From Betting on Casting and Release Dates
Studios and production companies have issued guidelines barring staff from prediction-market bets on earnings, casting and release dates, and one company set up an anonymous hotline to report colleagues.
The Hollywood Reporter learned that studios and production companies are quietly telling employees not to bet on prediction markets about studio earnings, casting or release dates, or to pass information to others who bet. PMC, which owns THR, Variety, Deadline and Dick Clark Productions, banned bets on award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates. BetOnline pulled its James Bond casting market this week after money moved sharply to Callum Turner. Betting on box office receipts is already illegal under the 1958 Onion Futures Act.
Potential Talent Implication: Casting choices and release dates now carry a cash price before they are announced, so everyone on a production with advance knowledge, the talent's own team included, is part of a leak risk studios are now policing.
The Facts
  • Studio guidelines (unnamed companies): no prediction-market bets on studio earnings, casting or release dates; no tipping friends or family; at least one company has an anonymous reporting hotline.
  • PMC handbook update (recent weeks): bans betting on "award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates."
  • Kalshi disclosed in February that a MrBeast video editor made $5,000 betting on confidential MrBeast content; fired and fined $20,000.
  • BetOnline temporarily pulled its James Bond casting market after "sharp money" moved Callum Turner above Jack Lowden.
  • Mitts and Ofir study (March): an estimated $143 million in anomalous profit on Polymarket over two years.
  • CFTC view: award-show bets (Oscars, Emmys) allowed as contests; game shows and reality competitions unresolved.
  • Onion Futures Act of 1958 bans only onion futures and motion picture box office receipts.
  • Joshua Mitts, Columbia Law: entertainment markets have "a high degree of asymmetric information" and "very little social utility."
· The Hollywood Reporter · Alex Weprin contributed · 2026-11-05 · https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/prediction-market-ban-hollywood-studios-1236742752/ · Provenance: reported-named-sources source ↗
Lionsgate Said 10 of Its Next 15 Wide Releases Are Franchises and Moved Its 3 Arts Stake Into a Joint Venture
Lionsgate grew revenue 41% to $668.8 million and adjusted OIBDA to $72.0 million from $14.1 million, cut leverage to 3.7x, and told investors 10 of its next 15 wide releases are franchises, with Sony now co-financing Naruto.
Lionsgate reported fiscal Q2 2027 revenue of $668.8 million, up 40.8 percent, and adjusted OIBDA of $72.0 million against $14.1 million a year ago [R]. Both segments grew: Motion Picture revenue rose 30.0 percent to $359.3 million on the Michael tail and the library, and Television rose 55.8 percent to $309.5 million on 22 scripted episode deliveries against seven [R] [call]. Leverage fell to 3.7x from 4.3x in one quarter [R]. CEO Jon Feltheimer said 10 of the next 15 wide releases are repeatable branded properties, and Sony won competitive bidding to co-finance and distribute Naruto internationally, with Destin Daniel Cretton directing from the spring [call]. In October SP Media bought into a new entity holding Lionsgate's 3 Arts interest, and the 3 Arts minority holders exercised their put on the remaining 24 percent at about $175.4 million [R]. CFO Jimmy Barge said about 58 percent of the $1.5 billion backlog is television because Lionsgate keeps back-end rights [call]. Michael 2 still has no production start or release date [call]. The quarter still lost $15.5 million on a reported basis [R]. Shares rose about 10.5 percent intraday on 11/6 [2nd].
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): With most film slots going to franchises and 3 Arts heading to full Lionsgate ownership, original filmmakers need a disciplined budget to get a slot, and 3 Arts clients should ask how conflicts are handled when their manager's owner is also the buyer.
The Facts
  • FQ2 FY27: revenue $668.8M (+40.8%), adjusted OIBDA $72.0M vs $14.1M, operating income $29.1M vs $(46.0)M, net loss $(15.5)M / $(0.05) per share [R].
  • Motion Picture $359.3M, segment profit $88.7M vs $30.5M; Television $309.5M, segment profit $21.6M vs $12.5M [R].
  • TTM library revenue $1.04B, second-highest ever [R]; backlog $1.5B [R], about 58% television [call].
  • Leverage 3.7x vs 4.3x in June [R]; net debt about $1.5B [call]; cash $358.5M, $800M revolver undrawn [R].
  • 3 Arts: SP Media holds a noncontrolling stake in the entity holding Lionsgate's 3 Arts interest; minority put on 24% at about $175.4M, closing by 2/1/27 [R].
  • Slate: 10 of the next 15 wide releases are franchises; Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens at Thanksgiving; Naruto with Sony starts production in the spring [call].
  • TV: The Hunting Wives season three ordered before season two premiered; Midnight Sun two-season adult animation at Netflix [call].
  • Adjusted free cash flow $(8.2)M in the quarter, $120.7M for six months [R].

California Turned Down the New Grey's Anatomy Spinoff Twice, So It Shoots in New Mexico a Season Late
ABC's untitled West Texas spinoff from Shonda Rhimes and Meg Marinis lost its California tax credit bid, then was told new shows could not reapply; it now preps in Albuquerque for the 2027-28 season.
The Grey's Anatomy franchise will film outside California for the first time in 23 years. ABC and 20th Television applied for the state film and TV tax credit for the spinoff this summer and were denied for not creating enough jobs. Waiting to reapply in the fall cost prep time, stage space and below-the-line crew, and then, Shondaland's Betsy Beers told an Assembly committee on October 29, they were told new shows could not apply. California's credit is capped at $750 million a year; Gavin Newsom proposed $1 billion this week.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): California scored the spinoff on the jobs it would add and gave no weight to two decades of Shondaland shows in Los Angeles, so Marinis, who also runs Grey's, runs two series in two states because of a credit decision she did not control.
The Facts
  • Show: untitled Grey's Anatomy spinoff, set at a rural West Texas medical center; ABC network, 20th Television studio, Shondaland. Created by Shonda Rhimes and Meg Marinis (current Grey's showrunner). EPs: Rhimes, Betsy Beers, Marinis, Ellen Pompeo.
  • Location: was to film in Los Angeles; now in pre-production in Albuquerque, New Mexico. First time the franchise films outside California in its 23-year history.
  • Schedule: pushed from midseason 2027 to the 2027-28 season.
  • Credit history: first application (summer 2026) denied, per Beers, "due to the fact we were not providing enough jobs for the state to consider us an asset." ABC and the studio planned to reapply in the fall, postponing prep and stage holds and losing below-the-line crew. Beers: "we were told, regardless of earlier messaging, there would be no chance to apply if you were a new show; returning, sure, not a new show."
  • Beers testimony: Assembly committee hearing, North Hollywood, October 29, 2026. Asked for a review of the award criteria and a larger pool. Shondaland's The Residence (Netflix) did receive a California credit.
  • Beers on proximity: "the co-creator and showrunner is also running Grey's, and the geographical proximity was key to her ability to doing the job."
  • Program: California Film and TV Tax Credit capped at $750 million a year. Governor Gavin Newsom proposed raising it to $1 billion a year (Monday, November 2). Los Angeles mayor-elect Nithya Raman (elected Tuesday, November 3) pledged a film czar and to push to uncap the program.

HBO's Deal Run Since the Merger Was Signed Before It, and HBO Is Still Bidding Against Netflix and Hulu
The Girls revival, the Crazy Rich Asians series and HBO's other pickups announced since Skydance closed on October 6 were negotiated before the close, sources told The Ankler; HBO is now in a live drama auction with Hulu and Netflix.
In the month since Skydance closed its purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, HBO announced a Girls revival, a Crazy Rich Asians series greenlight, a two-season order for an animated comedy and development of The Birds, a Sarah Snook limited series. Sources told The Ankler those deals predated the close. An HBO insider said the unit has been told neither that it has more money nor to stop spending. HBO is bidding against Hulu and Netflix for a drama, and Netflix preempted A24's Gwyneth Paltrow series The Apology with a two-season order before HBO heard the pitch.
Potential Talent Implication: HBO is still a third bidder on high-end drama, and the first new package it buys outright under Skydance will show whether that budget holds, since the run of announcements so far was business closed before the merger.
The Facts
  • Announced since the October 6 close: Girls revival; Crazy Rich Asians series greenlight; two-season order for an animated comedy; development of The Birds, a limited series led by Sarah Snook.
  • Sources: the Girls deal was "in the works for months"; Crazy Rich Asians "had a blinking green light and was on script approvals."
  • HBO insider: "We haven't been told we're in for a windfall and suddenly have more money, but we also haven't been told to stop spending money. We are full steam ahead."
  • Current bidding: HBO is in a bidding war with Hulu and Netflix for a drama (unnamed).
  • The Apology (Gwyneth Paltrow, A24): Netflix preemptively bought it with a two-season order before HBO's scheduled pitch.
  • The Spread (Javier Bardem drama): announced by HBO in September; closed months earlier after a bidding war that included Paramount+.
  • Source familiar with HBO: the announcements were held so HBO would look like it is "making stuff" after the close, despite about $80 billion in combined debt. HBO declined to comment.
  • Casey Bloys is Skydance's streaming chief.
  • Same column: Hulu won a six-way bidding war for Nick Paley's Phony (Connie Britton, Sam Nivola) after 20 production companies passed on the idea; Paley sold it with a two-minute sizzle reel. Disney expects layoffs to begin in the first quarter of 2027; Debra OConnell's TV reorganization is pending.

Bruno Dumont Made His Next Feature With Generative AI and No Actors After French Financing Dried Up
The two-time Cannes Grand Prix winner wrapped The End, an English-language sci-fi thriller, generating its images, performances and sound himself from his Paris home, and plans festivals and a 2027 theatrical release.
Bruno Dumont told Screen International his feature The End was made entirely with generative AI, without actors or a film crew, on what Screen calls a shoestring budget. He wrote the script more than 25 years ago and shelved it because its earthquake and asteroid sequences were too expensive to shoot. He began in August and has wrapped. He is producing independently, with no sales agent yet, and plans festival premieres before distribution. "It is becoming harder and harder to finance films in France," he said. A conventional live-action feature with Bathysphere Films is also in development.
Potential Talent Implication: Dumont got a 25-year-old script made by generating every performance himself, so an established director with a stalled project now has a way to finish it without a financier, and the actors who would have been cast are simply not in the budget.
The Facts
  • Director: Bruno Dumont (Cannes Grand Prix for Humanity, 1999, and Flanders, 2006; Berlinale Silver Bear jury prize for The Empire, 2024; Red Rocks premiered in Cannes Directors' Fortnight 2026).
  • Film: The End, English-language sci-fi thriller. A Los Angeles police officer investigates a crime as the city is hit by earthquakes and falling asteroids; set between Los Angeles and Joshua Tree.

What Talent Needs to Know 10 opportunities · 4 challenges
Opportunities
  • A documentary whose license reverts can now be rebuilt for a fraction of its original cost and sold again, which makes the reversion date and the right to make new versions of the film two of the most valuable terms in a nonfiction license. (Rights Ownership)
  • When one format brings in close to a third of a film's gross, the director who shoots for it is delivering a revenue line, which can give IMAX screen commitments and format exclusivity real weight in a filmmaker's deal. (Project Economics)
  • A single Spider-Man release moved Sony Pictures' quarterly profit more than sixfold, a figure that may carry weight for anyone negotiating on the next Spider-Man film, since the studio's reliance on the franchise is now in its own results. (Project Economics)
  • Sony's record is a film and franchise story while its TV production business shrank, so the open doors at Sony are franchise film and the new anime and live-action adaptation lane, not a bigger TV budget. (Project Economics)
  • With the largest exhibitor healthy and premium screens carrying a third of US admissions, filmmakers who shoot for large formats and filmmakers at Netflix have stronger grounds to ask for premium-screen commitments, full windows and box office bonuses. (Project Economics)
  • When IMAX screens carry nearly a third of a film's gross and streamers buy IMAX-only theatrical runs, an IMAX commitment becomes a deal term worth negotiating, from camera and budget to IMAX weeks and release-date protection. (Project Economics)
  • A horror filmmaker managed by Maxwell or Rowbotham now has a manager who also runs a Lionsgate buyer, so where a project is set up, and on what terms, may need to be shopped against other buyers before Render Road is the answer.
  • Lionsgate now builds its slate on properties it can repeat across film, stage, tours and games, so talent attached to a Lionsgate franchise is attached to more than one revenue line, and the participation terms decide which of those lines it shares in. (New Revenue Stream)
  • A home release no longer ends a big film's theatrical life, so a filmmaker's re-release terms, from format screens to how a second run's grosses count toward box office bonuses, are now worth writing into the deal. (Project Economics)
  • Letterboxd's 30 million monthly users and their ratings would sit with a news publisher rather than a studio, which keeps the largest film word-of-mouth platform outside any one distributor's control.
Challenges & Headwinds
  • With three animation labels under one owner and the Netflix order gone, the label a filmmaker's deal sits at, and the turnaround rights in it, may decide whether a project in development keeps a home.
  • When a buyer treats the theatrical run as marketing for its streaming service, the box office number that usually sets bonuses and backend no longer measures what the film earned the buyer, so the streaming performance terms carry the real value.
  • Because A24 sells foreign rights territory by territory, the overseas gross on an A24 hit mostly stays with regional distributors, which may cap what a filmmaker's backend can draw from it, and a sale would put those deals in a new owner's hands.
  • When one of the town's leading deal lawyers says studio films under $70 million lose money unless they are horror, a mid-budget drama or comedy may need a horror-sized budget, a tentpole's scale or outside financing to get made at a studio.
The Cocaine Cowboys Directors Got Their Film Back From Netflix and Remade It With AI for $200,000
Billy Corben and Alfred Spellman spent about $200,000 using AI to rework nearly 4,000 shots of their 2006 documentary after Netflix's license reverted, and are raising $5 million for a YouTube-first studio.
Rakontur, the Miami company behind Cocaine Cowboys, made documentaries for Netflix, HBO and Hulu until those buyers cut nonfiction spending. Rakontur Direct, with former Complex Networks CEO Rich Antoniello, targets 260 releases a year by its second year and will license shows to streamers only after they premiere on its own channels.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A documentary whose license reverts can now be rebuilt for a fraction of its original cost and sold again, which makes the reversion date and the right to make new versions of the film two of the most valuable terms in a nonfiction license.
The Facts

  • Rights: Cocaine Cowboys (2006), licensed to Netflix, reverted to Rakontur in 2026.

  • Recoup plan (Spellman): licensing, sponsorships and related programming, not YouTube ad revenue alone.
  • Rakontur Direct: seeking $5 million from strategic partners for about two years of operation; target 260 releases a year (about five a week) by year two; initial slate short-form, episodes of 15 minutes or less; first series A Sunny Place for Shady People; streamer licensing only after premiere on Rakontur's channels.
  • Hire: Rich Antoniello, co-founder and former CEO of Complex Networks (sold to BuzzFeed for $300 million in 2021).

  • Spellman: "AI is the third revolution we've lived through in this business."

Ken Ziffren Says Studio Films Under $70 Million Mostly Lose Money Unless They Are Horror
In his annual industry address, Ziffren Brittenham co-founder Ken Ziffren said a pay-one window can bring a studio as much as $250 million, and that wide releases rose to 94 this year.
Ziffren told a ballroom of entertainment lawyers that, outside horror, studio films costing under $70 million tend to lose money, which he said supports a tentpole investment strategy. He said wide releases fell from about 100 before Covid to 75 in 2024 and reached 94 in 2026, with the domestic box office headed to about $10 billion. Downstream, he said, the only distribution costs are remittance taxes, residuals and occasional profit participations. He backed the federal MPTER Act, which he said would bring $10 billion in production, and said AI will lower pre-production, post and production costs.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): When one of the town's leading deal lawyers says studio films under $70 million lose money unless they are horror, a mid-budget drama or comedy may need a horror-sized budget, a tentpole's scale or outside financing to get made at a studio.
The Facts
  • Box office outlook: about $10B domestic and nearly $36B global in 2026, the best since 2019.
  • Wide releases: about 100 pre-Covid, 75 in 2024, 94 in 2026.
  • Ziffren: outside horror, studio films costing under $70M tend to lose money.
  • Downstream: a pay-one window can bring up to $250M; after PVOD, studios license to sister ad-supported services. Quote: "The only costs in distribution are remittance taxes and residuals, and now and then profit participations."
  • MPTER Act (federal production credit, before Senate and House committees): eligible productions over $1M with 75% in the U.S.; Ziffren estimated "$10 billion" for the industry; he hoped it passes in the lame-duck session.
  • AI: will "lower the costs of post and pre-production, and ultimately production itself"; "AI was not a major issue as it was in 2023."

Disney's Startup Program Backed a Gray-Box AI Filmmaking Studio and a Fan Video Tool
Disney's 2026 Accelerator cohort includes Promise, whose gray-box system has AI build sets and props around actors in near real time, and OpenArt, a prompt video app Disney discussed for catalog songs and fan creations.
Disney showed its 2026 Accelerator cohort at a Demo Day in Burbank, TheWrap reported on November 4. Two of the five startups make filmmaking tools. Promise's MUSE system shoots actors in a neutral "gray box" and has AI fill in scenery and props, the method Doug Liman used on Bitcoin: Killing Satoshi; Promise said Disney has no gray-box project in work. OpenArt turns typed prompts into short videos, and Disney discussed it for catalog music videos, marketing and fan creations, screened by a CopySight infringement check. Cohort startups spend 15 weeks working inside Disney divisions.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Disney is testing tools that let marketers and fans generate new video from its catalog, which puts the weight on what existing contracts say about reuse of a performance, a voice or a song in footage nobody shot.
The Facts
  • Disney Accelerator began in 2014 and invests in startups that are further along in maturity; the 2026 cohort has five companies, each spending 15 weeks applying its product inside Disney, much of it at the theme parks.
  • Three cohort members are valued above $1 billion: Simile at $2 billion, FieldAI at $10 billion and Physical Intelligence at $20 billion.
  • Promise Advanced Imagination: AI-native studio; its MUSE operating system supports hybrid "gray box" shooting, where AI fills backgrounds and proxy props with digital scenery in near real time. CEO George Strompolos called gray-box shooting "still pretty cutting edge" and said Disney is not currently working on a gray-box project. Chief creative officer Dave Clark: "this allows me to just focus on the story, focus on the creative, and not worry about having to get my shots in a day."
  • Doug Liman's Bitcoin: Killing Satoshi (Gal Gadot, Pete Davidson, Casey Affleck, Isla Fisher) is cited as the first gray-box AI shoot.
  • OpenArt: prompt-to-video app working across multiple video models; CEO Coco Mao calls conversational instruction "vibe directing." Disney discussed it for new videos for older catalog soundtrack singles, marketing campaigns and user fan creations. It uses a CopySight tool that flags whether generated content risks infringing other IP.
  • TheWrap notes Disney warmed to fan creation after its "ill-fated" deal with OpenAI's Sora.
  • Simile surveys 20,000 to 50,000 people a week, holds a database of one million, and runs virtual focus groups of digital twins; Disney is using it to test its digital booking journey.

Supporters of the bipartisan Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act want it on the December 11 funding bill, and three of its Republican cosponsors lost their seats Tuesday.

Suno Told the Court an Artist's Name Is Just a Genre Label
In its first response to Jason Isbell's class action, Suno argued Tuesday that prompts invoking an artist's name are protected and that no state publicity law bars asking for "a Jason Isbell vibe."
Isbell, David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle sued in August, claiming Suno violates state right-of-publicity laws (control over commercial use of a person's identity) by letting users generate tracks that sound like specific artists, including through workarounds such as spacing out a name. Unlike the copyright suits Suno has faced and settled, this case rests on identity, which the plaintiffs say an artist keeps even after a catalog settlement or a training opt-in. Suno's attorney Andrew Gass called the theory a "shadow state law IP regime" that conflicts with federal law, which does not protect an artistic style.

The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: Jason Isbell, David Lowery, Guy Forsyth, Eduardo Calle; federal class action filed August 2026.
  • Claim: Suno violates state publicity laws and keeps artist "voiceprints" users can reach through prompts for "tone and phrasing," real names instead of stage names (the rapper Common), or spaced-out names ("t a y l o r s w i f t").

  • Suno: invoking an artist's name to describe a genre is protected by the First Amendment. "No state confers a right of publicity that prohibits a musician in a studio from saying to their producer, 'let's go for something here with more of a Jason Isbell vibe.'"

  • Kazan had a soft opening and a hit by week four, and Netflix answered with "Lonesome Dove," so a showrunner's standing at Netflix may rest on how a series grows after launch as much as on its first-week number.

Netflix Is Signing YouTube Creators to Fill the Hours Between Its Shows
Nielsen's Gauge put YouTube at 15.8% of U.S. TV time in August and Netflix at 7.7%, yet Antenna has Netflix churn at 2% against roughly 6% for its closest peers.
Julia Alexander argues in Puck that the Nielsen Gauge overstates a Netflix and YouTube rivalry: it counts a plumbing tutorial the same as "Stranger Things," and Netflix subscribers are not cancelling at higher rates. Omdia data she cites puts music videos at about a third of YouTube viewing time, news near 10% and podcasts about 5%, formats Netflix mostly does not carry. Her read is that Netflix's deals with Mark Rober, Ms. Rachel and Druski, and its video podcast licensing, aim to get subscribers opening the app outside primetime. Reed Hastings called YouTube a "highly tuned machine for attention."
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Netflix is paying for daily, lean-back formats it does not make itself, so a creator with a talk show, video podcast or kids series can sell Netflix on daytime use while keeping an audience on YouTube.
The Facts
  • Nielsen Gauge (released Oct. 22, for August): YouTube 15.8% of U.S. TV viewing; Netflix 7.7%, down from 9% last December.
  • Antenna: Netflix churn steady at 2%; closest peers about 6%.
  • Hub Entertainment Research: about 80% of U.S. YouTube users said they sometimes or frequently turn to YouTube when they cannot find something on another streamer.
  • Omdia: music videos about a third of YouTube viewing time; news about 10%; podcasts about 5%.
  • Enders Analysis (U.K.): viewers added about 13 minutes of daily YouTube over two years while Netflix engagement held flat; exposure concentrated in low-propensity Netflix subscribers.
  • Netflix creator and format deals cited: Mark Rober, Ms. Rachel, licensed video podcasts, and the Druski deal announced Nov. 2 (Druski is set to host "Saturday Night Live").
  • YouTube: ad revenue growth in single digits per Alphabet's latest results; YouTube Premium and Music above 150 million subscribers; more than a third of YouTube ad revenue comes from TV sets.
  • ESPN and Pat McAfee: about 464,000 average viewers across TV and digital in September; all three hours stream on YouTube while ESPN linear carries two.
  • Reed Hastings (Kara Swisher's On podcast): YouTube is a "highly tuned machine for attention" that is "winning viewing hours."

Blumhouse Atomic Made $1.3 Billion This Year on Films That Cost Under $70 Million
Jason Blum and James Wan renamed their merged company Blumhouse Atomic and said this year's films, led by Curry Barker's "Obsession" and Kane Parsons' "Backrooms," earned nearly $1.3 billion on under $70 million in budgets.
Two years after merging, Blumhouse and Atomic Monster now operate as Blumhouse Atomic, keeping both labels and their separate creative teams. The company says its films have grossed more than $2.5 billion worldwide since the merger on combined production budgets under $330 million. "Obsession" and "Backrooms" became the highest-grossing films for Focus Features and A24. It hired Shudder's Sam Zimmerman to find new filmmakers and make movies under $5 million, and it regained the "Saw" rights, with Lionsgate keeping its existing ownership and distribution. Blum named television, games and live experiences as the next markets.
Potential Talent Implication: Curry Barker and Kane Parsons each gave their distributor its biggest film of the year on a Blumhouse Atomic budget, and the company is now hiring to find more filmmakers like them for movies under $5 million.
The Facts
  • New name: Blumhouse Atomic, for the combined Blumhouse and Atomic Monster. Both continue as distinct production labels with their own creative teams.
  • Company figures: more than $2.5 billion global box office since the merger on combined production budgets under $330 million; more than $1 billion worldwide in each of 2025 and 2026; this year's films nearly $1.3 billion on under $70 million in production budgets.
  • Hits: Curry Barker's "Obsession" (highest-grossing film for Focus Features) and Kane Parsons' "Backrooms" (highest-grossing film for A24).
  • Hiring: Sam Zimmerman (from Shudder), SVP development and acquisitions, to "discover frosh filmmakers and make movies with budgets under $5M." He was involved in Universal buying Joshua Giuliano's "River" from IFC for $10 million-plus at TIFF.
  • Deals: first-look with Divide/Conquer (late 2025) for high-concept, cost-efficient genre films. "Saw" rights acquired last year; Lionsgate retains existing ownership and distribution rights; Content Partners and Mark Burg hold interests in the existing film library.
  • 2027 slate: "River," "The Revenge of La Llorona," "The Exorcist: Martyrs," "Anything But Ghosts," "Paranormal Activity," "Molepeople," "Blair Witch," "Sleepover," "Seasons."
  • TV and other: USA's "The Rainmaker," Prime Video's "Scarpetta," Netflix's "Worst Ever" franchise; the game "Grave Seasons"; "Paranormal Activity" on Broadway; Universal Halloween Horror Nights collaborations.
  • Jason Blum: "We have the output of a studio with the creative freedom and financial discipline of an independent company, and more opportunities than ever to take these stories beyond the theater and into television, games and live experiences."
  • James Wan: "The future of horror comes from new voices, and Blumhouse Atomic gives us more ways to find them and support them for the long haul."
  • Separately (The Verge, Nov. 3): Curry Barker released a new horror short on YouTube.

Newsom Proposed a $1 Billion Film Credit That Would Cover Talent Salaries
Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed lifting California's annual film and TV credit from $750 million to at least $1 billion, opening it to above-the-line pay and extending it through 2040.
Newsom's Nov. 2 proposal raises the program to at least $1 billion a year and extends eligibility to above-the-line compensation (pay for actors, directors, writers and producers), subject to funding caps. It also reserves $100 million a year for independent productions, up $26 million, adds a 5% credit boost for companies committing to at least two California productions, and moves the sunset from 2030 to 2040. The push will fall to the next governor and the Legislature, THR reported. ProdPro data cited by THR has New York production spending up 87% in the latest quarter against California's 17%.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): If above-the-line pay becomes eligible, a large star or director salary could stop counting against a California shoot and become part of what the state helps pay for.
The Facts
  • Proposal (governor's release, Nov. 2): annual credit from $750 million to "at least" $1 billion; above-the-line talent compensation eligible, "subject to funding caps"; $100 million a year for independent productions (up $26 million); 5% credit boost for companies committing to at least two distinct qualifying California productions; sunset extended from five years to 10, through 2040.
  • Last year's expansion took the credit from $330 million to $750 million ($3.75 billion over five years through 2030). In its first expanded year, per the release: applications up 82%, $8.25 billion in direct production spending, film shoot days up 52%, TV shoot days up more than 7%, more than 43,000 cast and crew jobs.
  • Newsom asked Congress to pass the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA) by year end and backed a 20% federal credit that would stack with state programs.
  • Newsom: "At least $1 billion in tax credits means more investment flowing into our economy and more opportunity across the industry... But states can't shoulder the cost alone."
  • THR: the follow-through falls to the next governor, likely Xavier Becerra if he defeats Steve Hilton on Nov. 3.
  • ProdPro (October report, via THR): California $6.06 billion in production spend over 12 months vs. New York $4.63 billion; New York up 87% in the latest quarter vs. California 17%; New York had 17 live-action features budgeted over $10 million shooting last quarter vs. 13 for California.
  • Recent credits (Oct. 7 round, via THR): untitled Pixar animated feature $40.1 million, Lionsgate's "Michael" sequel $30.8 million, untitled Paramount crime thriller $29.3 million; "The Pitt" $24.2 million.
  • California Film Commission director Colleen Bell (outgoing) and Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur both backed the call.
  • Recently signed state law also adds a post-production credit, disclosure rules for ads using AI-generated performers, and stronger digital likeness protections including for deceased performers.

WME Told the OpenAI Court That AI Training Should Be Licensed, Not Stopped
WME's Oct. 30 amicus brief in the New York Times case against OpenAI says creators should decide whether, and on what terms, their work trains AI, and cites 28 paid data deals.
WME filed an amicus brief (a friend-of-the-court filing) on Oct. 30 in the consolidated copyright case brought by the New York Times and others against OpenAI. The agency's position is that AI use of creative work "should be licensed," not stopped, and that any use affecting talent's rights needs compensation and authorization. The brief cites at least 28 paid training-data deals between mid-2023 and mid-2024 and says AI developers are now shopping for licenses to film and TV libraries. SAG-AFTRA, the AFM and both WGAs filed a joint brief on Oct. 29; the Justice Department backed OpenAI in September.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): WME is now on the record that a paid market for training on its clients' work already exists, and the open question is whether the court treats that market as one OpenAI was obliged to use.
The Facts
  • Filed: Oct. 30, 2026, amicus brief by WME Group legal chief Courtney Braun and outside firm Jayaram PLLC; 18 pages (Deadline).
  • WME: "WME's position is therefore not that AI use of creative materials should be stopped, but that it should be licensed."
  • WME: "any use of AI that affects talents' and creators' rights must come with proper compensation and authorization"; it "seeks to preserve the legal framework that lets creators decide whether, and on what terms, their protected work is used to develop or train AI systems."
  • Brief: between mid-2023 and mid-2024, more than two dozen licensing deals or partnerships were announced, at least 28 involving payment for training data, including News Corp's reported five-year, $250 million agreement with OpenAI, Reddit's $60 million deal with Google, and Shutterstock's reported $25 million to $50 million deals with each of Apple, Amazon and Google.
  • Brief: "that market has grown as AI developers continue to actively shop for licenses to film and television libraries."
  • Deadline calls WME the first major Hollywood agency to enter this case. SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians and the WGA East and West filed a joint brief Oct. 29.
  • The Justice Department filed in September: "The United States has a strong interest in this Court rejecting any argument that training LLMs on copyrighted texts violates copyright law."
  • The case is nearly three years old; the Times alleges OpenAI built "substitutive products without permission or payment."

  • Fitch: debt-to-EBITDA 7.8 times; analyst Wunmi Adekanmbi: "this is not going to be organic deleveraging." Fitch and S&P rate the company BB; Moody's Ba3.
  • S&P's Naveen Sarma: "We don't have them generating cash flow in '26 and '27. Only in '28 do they begin to generate cash flow."
  • Linear TV is about two-thirds of company EBITDA.
  • Savings levers named by analysts: real estate, procurement, marketing, technology, layoffs; inside content: "shelving projects, cutting any duplicate overall and first-look deals, using AI to lower production costs or being more efficient with where they produce content."
  • Citi's Jason Bazinet expects $8 billion in savings by 2029. MoffettNathanson's Robert Fishman expects heavy spend on "must-have" sports rights and more third-party licensing to fund at least 30 theatrical releases a year. Skydance produced more than 180 series in 2026.
  • Equity: Elon Musk $1 billion, Laurene Powell Jobs $250 million, Shinsegae $1 billion; 471 million warrants at a $12 exercise price could raise about $5.7 billion.
  • Labor: about 2,000 layoffs after the Paramount merger; an LA County study projects nearly 4,500 local film and TV jobs affected over three years. Skydance has offered voluntary buyouts and moved to five days a week in office.
  • Skydance spokesperson: the company has "significant scale and free cash flow generation" to support its priorities.

California Lawmakers Floated a Tax Credit on Actor and Director Salaries
At an Oct. 29 Assembly hearing, members discussed lifting the $750 million cap on California's film credit and subsidizing above-the-line pay, which the program now excludes.
An Assembly select committee met in North Hollywood on Oct. 29 to discuss removing the cap on California's $750 million film and TV credit, which projects compete for in periodic windows. Chair Rick Chavez Zbur said he wants to raise or eliminate the cap next session but called it "a heavy lift" given the state deficit. Assemblyman Nick Schultz floated extending the program past its 2030 sunset and subsidizing above-the-line costs (salaries for actors, directors and other key creatives). Betsy Beers testified that a "Grey's Anatomy" spinoff lost out on the credit and is shooting in Albuquerque.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): California's credit does not cover what actors and directors are paid, and adding those salaries, as one lawmaker proposed, would change the math most for productions with large above-the-line budgets.
The Facts
  • Hearing: Assembly Select Committee on Growing and Retaining the Creative Economy in California, North Hollywood, Oct. 29 (Variety).
  • Program: $750 million annual cap; base credit raised from 20% to 35% last year; cap raised from $330 million; sunsets in 2030. Projects apply in windows and are ranked on a "jobs ratio" score.
  • Rick Chavez Zbur (chair): "I think either increasing the cap or eliminating it... But you know that is a heavy lift." He floated "dynamic scoring" of the credit's return.
  • Nick Schultz floated extending the sunset date, subsidizing above-the-line costs (salaries for actors, directors, etc.), and opening eligibility to commercials and game shows.
  • Betsy Beers (Shondaland): a "Grey's Anatomy" spinoff set in West Texas did not get the credit in two tries (scored too low, then the program was oversubscribed); "now we are filming in Albuquerque."
  • Georgia's credit has no limit; New York can borrow from future-year allocations.
  • Legislative Analyst's Office economist Rowan Isaaks: research shows film credits return 20 to 50 cents per state dollar; a more generous credit "might mean fewer projects overall." LAEDC (MPA-funded study): $1.07 return.
  • FilmLA: LA-area production volume continues to fall even as the share of scripted shows with a state subsidy has nearly doubled. Congress is considering a 20% national incentive.

Record Labels Are Worth $20 Billion Less as New Artists Ask to Own Their Music
Universal Music and Warner Music shares are down about 30% over five years, more than $20 billion in value, and UMG management discussed going private with Blackstone, TPG and Apollo earlier this year.
Lucas Shaw reports in Bloomberg's Screentime that Universal Music Group management held informal take-private talks with Blackstone, TPG and Apollo, mostly in the first half of 2026, with no formal sale process. UMG's enterprise value is $36 billion; the Bolloré family owns about 30% and rejected Bill Ackman's merger proposal. Shaw writes that new acts now have more leverage before signing and want ownership from the start, and that independent distributors will release music without taking ownership, pushing labels toward more artist-friendly deals. Catalogs still sell privately at 20 to 30 times earnings.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A catalog an artist owns still sells for 20 to 30 times earnings, and independent distributors will now release a debut without taking it, which puts ownership of the masters on the table in a first label deal.
The Facts
  • UMG and Warner Music Group shares: down about 30% over five years, more than $20 billion of market value lost; S&P 500 up about 65% over the same span (Bloomberg).
  • UMG management discussed a take-private with Blackstone, TPG and Apollo Global Management; informal, mostly in the first half of 2026; no formal sales process (Bloomberg; first reported 10/26).
  • UMG enterprise value: $36 billion including debt. Bolloré family owns about 30%; rejected Bill Ackman's merger proposal. Cyrille Bolloré, May: "We can't sell too early."
  • Global recorded music sales rose from $14 billion (2014) to about $21 billion (2020); major artists sold catalogs at 20 to 30 times earnings.
  • Len Blavatnik bought Warner for $3.3 billion in 2011 and raised nearly $2 billion selling about 77 million shares at the IPO. Lucian Grainge made more than $300 million in 2021 on an IPO-tied bonus.
  • Shaw: acts "aren't interested in signing away ownership of their first six albums"; independent distributors support releases "without demanding ownership."
  • Michael Morris (Guggenheim): "A dollar of catalog revenue is worth more."
  • Grainge on the Q3 call: UMG is working to get streaming services to pay more for the most popular artists and less for AI tracks. UMG cut hundreds of jobs in recent weeks; shares up about 20% over the last month after Q3 beat estimates.
  • Same edition: YouTube ad sales grew 9% last quarter; YouTube passed 150 million subscribers across TV, Music and Premium.

Anime Production Houses Now Take Equity in Their Shows to Share in $16 Billion of Overseas Sales
Overseas sales reached $16.1 billion of Japan's $28.18 billion anime business in 2025, but only $3.2 billion flowed back to the companies that make the shows.
Japan's anime industry grew 15.8% to $28.18 billion in 2025, according to the Association of Japanese Animations (AJA), presented at TIFFCOM. Overseas revenue rose 17% to $16.1 billion, about 57% of the total; domestic revenue rose just over 14% to $12 billion. Revenue reaching production companies, as distinct from the production committees (the investor groups that finance and own most anime), rose 8% to $3.2 billion. AJA's Masahiro Hasegawa said more production companies now take an equity position in their works to keep the IP and share in overseas revenue.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The companies that make anime collect about $3.2 billion of a $28 billion business, and the route to a larger share is equity in the title itself, which carries the overseas revenue a production fee never touches.
The Facts
  • Japan anime industry 2025: $28.18 billion (JPY4.45 trillion), up 15.8% (AJA Anime Industry Report, presented at TIFFCOM).
  • Overseas revenue: $16.1 billion (JPY2.54 trillion), about 57% of the total, up 17%. Domestic: $12 billion (JPY1.9 trillion), 43%, up just over 14%.
  • 2024 comparison: overseas sales grew 26% while domestic was mostly flat. Overseas first overtook domestic in 2020.
  • Revenue flowing back to anime production companies (not production committees): $3.2 billion (JPY505 billion) in 2025 vs $2.95 billion (JPY466 billion) in 2024, up 8%.
  • Masahiro Hasegawa, editor-in-chief of AJA's Anime Industry Report: more production companies are taking an equity position in their works, holding on to IP and participating in overseas revenue.
  • Demon Slayer: Kimetsu No Yaiba The Movie, Infinity Castle grossed about $800 million worldwide in 2025, the highest-grossing Japanese film of all time. Chiikawa The Movie has grossed about $159 million worldwide in 2026.
  • Japan's IP360 initiative targets $127 billion (JPY20 trillion) in content exports by 2033, including $38 billion (JPY6 trillion) for anime.

CAA and Hollywood Stars Told the OpenAI Court a Licensing Market for Their Work Already Exists
The Human Consent Foundation, CAA and voice-actor and music groups filed a 31-page brief in The New York Times case against OpenAI and Microsoft, signed by stars including Scarlett Johansson, Robert De Niro and Julia Roberts.
The Human Consent Foundation, a nonprofit Cate Blanchett co-founded, filed an amicus brief (an outside party's argument to the court) on Friday in the Southern District of New York, joined by CAA, the Music Artists Coalition, the National Association of Voice Actors, Writer, Inc and the Creative Coalition on AI. It answers OpenAI and Microsoft's claim that licensing training data is cost-prohibitive and impossible to value: "The creative industries already have in place a proven infrastructure and workflows to clear rights for dispersed works at scale." OpenAI points to briefs backing fair use, including one from the U.S. government.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Whether a court accepts that a working market for licensing a face, voice or script already exists decides whether AI training is something talent gets paid for or something talent cannot stop.

  • Blanchett: "If someone wants to use my face, my voice or my image, they ask me first. There is a contract. There is a conversation."
  • Hexum: "There is already a functioning market and infrastructure for licensing creative work."

Flawless's AI Dubbing Tools, Built on Actor Consent, Were Sold in a UK Insolvency
Administrator BTG sold the TrueSync dubbing and DeepEditor tools to TBellScout, a startup owned by Elastic founder Steven Schuurman, after Flawless Holdings filed for administration this month.
Flawless raised $100 million from wealthy individuals to build AI dubbing tools endorsed by SAG-AFTRA and used on hundreds of Hollywood productions, including Fall and Watch the Skies. Its UK company, Flawless Holdings, filed for administration (the UK equivalent of Chapter 11, run by an outside insolvency firm) earlier in October. BTG, appointed by lender Sprk Capital, sold TrueSync and DeepEditor to TBellScout, owned by Dutch billionaire Steven Schuurman, who confirmed the deal to Deadline. Co-founders Scott Mann and Nick Lynes still control Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. company that held the studio relationships.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Flawless's consent-based approach lived in its studio relationships, and the tools have gone to a buyer without those relationships, so the protection that travels with a dubbed performance is the AI language in the actor's own contract.
The Facts
  • Flawless spent $100 million, raised from wealthy individuals rather than venture capital, building SAG-AFTRA-endorsed AI dubbing technology.
  • Assets sold: TrueSync (visual dubbing; named one of Time's Best Inventions) and DeepEditor (AI post-production; changes dialogue and performance without reshoots). Buyer: TBellScout, owned by Steven Schuurman, founder of Elastic. Schuurman confirmed the acquisition and declined further comment.
  • Seller: Flawless Holdings Limited (UK trading company, founded 2020), which filed for administration earlier in October. Administrator BTG was appointed by Sprk Capital, a UK tech lender holding fixed and floating charges over Flawless.
  • Flawless's third tool, the rights management platform Artistic Rights Treasury, is not named among the assets sold.
  • Scott Mann and Nick Lynes remain in control of Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. business that built the studio relationships on a consent-based approach; they are said to be exploring a new venture. Amit Kapur became co-CEO in March.
  • Credits: Fall (AI used to remove swearing for a PG-13), Watch the Skies (first theatrical feature with immersive AI dubbing, released with XYZ Films), The Book of Solutions, Tatami, Smugglers, Vincent Must Die, The Light. Studios have largely declined to disclose their AI use.

Meta's New Business Terms Would Let It Scrape Business Accounts for Its Products With No Opt-Out
The Copyright Alliance called the terms "unconscionable," a court in Oslo temporarily barred them, and Meta said the Nov. 20 start could slip again pending industry consultation.
Meta's updated business terms would apply to commercial accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads and WhatsApp. The current draft lets Meta use scrapers and crawlers "to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products"; an earlier draft also said "train" and was revised after publisher pushback. The Copyright Alliance, whose members include the RIAA, NMPA, Universal Music Group, ASCAP and BMI, said the terms still allow broad scraping for generative AI, let Meta ignore robots.txt (the standard do-not-crawl signal), and offer no opt-out. Meta says content owners can still use robots.txt.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Every production company and creator brand runs a Meta business account, so if these terms take effect, keeping work out of Meta's products could come down to closing the account.
The Facts
  • Terms: updated commercial terms for business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Threads, WhatsApp; effective date moved from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20 on Oct. 23; Meta now says the consultation "could extend beyond November 20, in which case we'd delay implementation." Reuters reported an indefinite delay.
  • Earlier draft (reported by Nieman Lab Oct. 15): Meta "may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of" its products. Current draft drops "train."
  • Copyright Alliance (Oct. 27), CEO Keith Kupferschmid: the terms "could allow Meta to scrape any business user's content and use that scraped content, much of which is protected by copyright, in Meta's own business products, including for advertising, and to train and ground the company's AI products." No opt-out; accept or terminate the account.
  • Meta (Andy Stone, VP Communications, Oct. 28): "We do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders." To Reuters: "content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences."
  • Oslo court (Oct. 28) temporarily barred implementation on a challenge from ten Norwegian media groups including NRK and Schibsted, pending a final ruling.
  • Earlier complaints from publishers and advertisers to EU and UK antitrust authorities (Reuters).
  • Letters: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (Oct. 23) and Sen. Adam Schiff (Oct. 24).
  • Copyright Alliance says it represents more than two million individual creators and 15,000 organizations.

The Guilds Told the OpenAI Court a Fair Use Ruling Would Void Their AI Licensing Terms
SAG-AFTRA, the WGA East and West and the AFM filed a 34-page amicus brief Thursday in the New York copyright case against OpenAI, citing the AI bargaining right they won this year.
The four unions asked the federal court hearing the consolidated case brought by the New York Times, other outlets and authors including George R.R. Martin and John Grisham to reject a categorical fair use exemption (a blanket legal permission) for training AI models. The brief says the 2026 contracts gave writers and actors a notice-and-bargaining right over third-party licenses of covered work for AI training, and that a ruling that training is fair use "would render moot the terms the unions and the industry agreed to at the bargaining table." Fair use, the unions argue, must stay a case-by-case call.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The AI terms the guilds won in 2026 pay off only if training needs a license, so whether actors and writers are ever paid when their work trains a model may turn on this ruling as much as on any contract.
The Facts
  • Filers: SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians, the Writers Guild of America East and West. Joint amicus brief, filed Thursday, October 29, 2026; 34 pages.
  • Case: consolidated copyright action in New York federal court against OpenAI. Plaintiffs include the New York Times, Florida and Arkansas papers, The Intercept, Sarah Silverman, the Authors Guild, and authors Ta-Nehisi Coates, George R.R. Martin, John Grisham, Michael Connelly, Jonathan Franzen and Jodi Picoult, among others.
  • Ask: reject a categorical fair use exemption for AI training; decide fair use case by case.
  • Brief: "The harms of unlicensed training fall not just on companies like the News Plaintiffs, but on the countless professionals behind the work."
  • Brief: a blanket exemption would allow a "potentially enormous transfer of value" from creators to corporations.
  • Contract hook: in 2026 negotiations the writers and actors guilds won a notice-and-bargaining right for third-party licenses of covered work used to train commercial generative AI systems.
  • Brief: "These negotiated provisions presuppose that training on covered work is a use that can be licensed and that the people whose work is used have a stake in the terms."

European Producers Say Netflix's Local Shows Come With Worse Terms Than Their Broadcasters
Netflix keeps the rights in every territory on its local originals, and no French scripted original besides Lupin has reached four seasons, producers told The Ankler.
In a report on what Peter Rice inherits as Netflix's new chief content officer, European producers said the "local for local" strategy limits their businesses. Robert Franke, former head of drama at ZDF Studios, said Netflix typically keeps the rights in every territory, while a show made for a local broadcaster can be sold abroad through distributors, potentially for more money. Pernel Media CEO Samuel Kissous said Netflix pays high budgets but orders few seasons. Netflix spent €308 million on French content, second only to France Télévisions. What Talent Needs to Know 8 opportunities · 2 challenges
Opportunities
  • In New York and New Jersey a star's fee counts toward the credit and lowers the picture's net cost, and in California it does not, which makes the cast attachment part of the location math on any studio film shooting in the U.S. (Project Economics)

  • Hammond is developing his own story in two formats before any buyer is attached, so the format carve-out (vertical rights sold separately from film rights) decides how much of the story he still controls after the first sale. (Rights Ownership)

New York and New Jersey Count Star Salaries in Their Film Credits and California Does Not
Congress returns Nov. 9 aiming to pass the federal film credit by Dec. 18; New York's 30 percent credit counts above-the-line pay, while California's $750 million program still excludes it.
Backers of the Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act expect it to pass in the lame-duck session that opens Nov. 9, before a Dec. 18 Senate adjournment target; the IRS would run it. Film commissioners and studio executives told TheWrap that other states, not California, may collect the surge. New York and New Jersey count above-the-line salaries (pay for stars, directors, writers and producers) toward their credits. California raised its cap from $330 million to $750 million but still excludes them, and one unnamed studio executive said it "wouldn't be in my top 5 states to shoot."
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): In New York and New Jersey a star's fee counts toward the credit and lowers the picture's net cost, and in California it does not, which makes the cast attachment part of the location math on any studio film shooting in the U.S.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act; built on U.S. labor costs; would stack on state incentives. President Trump endorsed the idea in early September.
  • Timing: Congress returns Nov. 9; government funding deadline Dec. 11; targeted Senate adjournment Dec. 18. Congressional insiders say the IRS would run it, with no new federal film commission.
  • Union-commissioned study: major-studio production spending located in the U.S. fell from 74% in 1999 to 42% in 2024.
  • New York: $800 million cap plus a separate $100 million indie program; above-the-line spending counts toward the 30% base credit, up to a 40% limit of other qualified costs.
  • New Jersey: 30% base including above-the-line, up to 44% with bonuses; a $250 million program for studios that lease stages in the state (Netflix, Lionsgate, Paramount at 1888 Studios in Bayonne).
  • Georgia: uncapped; output fell from 412 productions and $4.4 billion of direct spending in 2022 to 245 productions and $2.3 billion in 2025.
  • California: cap raised to $750 million; above-the-line excluded; projects must start shooting within 180 days of approval; a 2027 push to uncap is expected. Mayor Karen Bass supports uncapping.
  • David Ellison (Skydance): "Even if you got the federal rebate, California would not be as competitive with some of the other states in the United States. Jersey is at 43%. Georgia is at 38%."
  • Scott Karol (SP Media Group): "We don't need to have the best tax credit. We just need a competitive one."
  • Thomas Laub (Shadowbox Studios, Georgia) on stability: the U.K. credit has been stable for 20 years; the worry is "two, three golden years" followed by repeal.

The memo, obtained by Deadline, phases in a five-day office week across Skydance, which closed its $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery this month; Warner staff had been on three days. Puck's Kim Masters reports, citing unnamed executives, that Elon Musk's $1 billion investment alarmed people on the Warner lot, and one high-value creative with business there described fear. Masters expects Skydance to spend to show it is talent-friendly, within what its debt allows. Senator Ron Wyden called the investment "an unholy alliance."
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Skydance is trying to show it is still a place talent wants to work while it cuts $2 billion and services its debt, and the creatives it most wants are the ones who can set the price of that proof.
The Facts
  • Memo from co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreitz (10/26): five-day in-office policy across Skydance, phased by location (largest sites: Los Angeles, New York, Atlanta, London); Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program with individual terms and a decision window.
  • Paramount had already returned to five days; WBD was at three.
  • Skydance closed its $110 billion acquisition of WBD earlier in October; combined debt near $90 billion (Deadline); Puck cites an $80 billion debt load and $6 billion in synergies.
  • Ellison has committed to at least $2 billion in cost savings, part from layoffs (Deadline).
  • Elon Musk invested $1 billion in Skydance; John Malone predicted SpaceX could invest up to $10 billion (Puck).
  • Puck (unnamed exec): "People are freaking out." Masters: Skydance "can, and likely will, counter by throwing piles of money around to establish its talent-friendliness."
  • Alex Gibney's documentary Musk is still set for HBO Max in early 2027 (Puck, HBO source).
  • Malone said Netflix was told by the administration it had no chance of regulatory approval for its WBD bid (Puck; Netflix declined to comment).

Reed Hastings told Kara Swisher Netflix should answer its viewing slowdown with "more and better television shows, more and better movies," and said Netflix chose not to raise its Warner Bros. bid.

Japan's $5 Million Floor Is Keeping Smaller Shoots Out of Its Incentive
Tokyo Vice producer Alex Boden said Japan's IP360 incentive now requires about $5 million of local spend while most Japanese films cost $1.5 million to $3 million; Netflix asked for certainty over size.
IP360 replaced the JLOX scheme, which offered up to a 50 percent cash rebate and drew Tokyo Vice, Rental Family and Drops of God to Japan. At an MPA seminar at the Tokyo International Film Festival, Boden said the new floor excludes independent and lower-budget projects, that Shogun and Pachinko scouted Japan and shot elsewhere, and that a panel decides awards. Netflix APAC production affairs director Debra Richards said a lower incentive is fine "so long as it's certain" and called the current one opaque.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Under $5 million of local spend, a Japan-set project gets no IP360 money, and above it a panel decides case by case, which keeps the rebate out of the financing plan until it is approved.
The Facts
  • IP360, run by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), replaced JLOX (introduced 2022, up to 50 percent cash rebate on qualifying spend). METI target: $127 billion (JPY20 trillion) in Japanese content exports by 2033.
  • Minimum spend raised to about $5 million (JPY800 million) of Japan spend; Boden: most Japanese films cost $1.5 million to $3 million.
  • Improvements Boden credited: more funds, more projects supported, a two-year application window.
  • Boden's asks: lower the floor, widen which producers may apply, automatic approval in place of a panel.
  • Debra Richards (Netflix, Director APAC Content & Studio Production Affairs): "You could have a lower incentive, that's fine, so long as it's certain and the criteria are clear."
  • Shogun and Pachinko scouted Japan and shot elsewhere. Productions that shot under JLOX (Rental Family, Drops of God, Neuromancer, Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!) did so before the changes.
  • Event: MPA seminar 'Strengthening Japan's Production Environment' at the Tokyo International Film Festival (runs to November 4).
