Netflix's True-Story Shows Are Drawing Defamation Suits That Survive Early Dismissal
On October 20 a Florida judge let two Miami officers' defamation suit over The Rip proceed, and Netflix withdrew its Baby Reindeer appeal, sending Fiona Harvey's case back to the trial court.
Judge Daryl Trawick refused to dismiss claims by officers Jason Smith and Jonathan Santana against Falco Pictures, which registration records tie to Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity. He ruled that whether the film's heroic second half cures the portrayal is a jury question, and let an emotional distress claim proceed. Netflix holds The Rip's copyright but is not a defendant. Separately, a Ninth Circuit en banc ruling barred interim federal appeals of anti-SLAPP (early dismissal of speech suits) denials, so Netflix dropped its Baby Reindeer appeal.
Potential Talent Implication: The producers, not Netflix, are the named defendants on The Rip, so on a fictionalized true story the indemnity and errors and omissions terms decide who pays for depositions and discovery when a real person recognizes themselves.
The Facts
  • The Rip: Netflix film starring and produced by Ben Affleck and Matt Damon, a fictionalized account of a 2016 Miami police raid that recovered $20 million in drug money.
  • Plaintiffs: officers Jason Smith and Jonathan Santana. Filed in federal court in May; withdrawn and refiled in Florida state court.
  • Defendant: Falco Pictures, which registration records indicate is owned and operated by Artists Equity. Netflix holds the copyright and is not a defendant.
  • Ruling (Judge Daryl Trawick, October 20): defamatory reading is a jury question; plaintiffs adequately alleged the film is "of and concerning" them; portrayal could support actual malice; depicting officers lying to obtain consent to search could be defamation per se; intentional infliction of emotional distress claim proceeds.
  • Baby Reindeer: September 2024, a federal judge in Los Angeles denied Netflix's anti-SLAPP motion against Fiona Harvey, noting the episode one title card "This is a true story."   • Disclosure in the piece: RedBird Capital is an investor in Puck and in Artists Equity.

Studios Are Weighing a 4 Percent Tax Credit Cut Over California's Diversity Rules
Productions that skip California's diversity program keep 96 percent of their tax credit; Universal's production CFO told the film commission the studio has considered opting out, citing federal law.
At a June 5 California Film Commission meeting reviewed by THR, Arturo Barquet, CFO of global production operations at Universal, said parts of the program conflict with federal law and that Paramount was not taking part; a person familiar says Skydance has no blanket policy against it. Sony's Andrew Davis called compliance a "tremendous burden." The program has no quotas and grades good-faith effort under incentives Newsom doubled to $750 million. 105 of 115 productions opted in over eight windows. Universal's Snoop Dogg biopic stands to receive $17 million in credits.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): On a $17 million credit, opting out costs about $680,000, the price a studio now weighs against the hiring plan and assessments a producer must deliver to keep the full California credit.
The Facts
  • Opt-out or non-compliance: production still qualifies for 96 percent of its allocated credit.
  • Requirements under the expanded rules: checklist covering hiring, workplace education, workforce development and supplier diversity; a plan to broaden access to jobs; an interim assessment before filming; a final assessment after production. No quotas or hiring targets.
  • California incentive raised from $330 million to $750 million last year.
  • Participation: 105 of 115 productions opted in across the past eight application windows (commission figure).
  • Arturo Barquet (Universal Filmed Entertainment): Universal has "many times considered whether we should opt out"; "there are things in here that are in conflict with federal law"; said his understanding is Paramount is not going for the program.
  • Barquet said an untitled Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert film was rejected three times and the Snoop Dogg biopic twice before approval. Snoop expected to receive $17 million (lower if the program is not completed).
  • Andrew Davis (Sony Pictures, president of production administration): compliance is a "tremendous burden on both television and features."
  • UCLA: minority lead actors on streaming fell from 51 percent (2024) to 36 percent (2025).
  • Calculation: 4 percent of $17 million = $680,000.

Talent Departures Pushed Sarandos to Fire Netflix's Content and Film Chiefs
Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw reports that Dan Lin passed on projects from partners including Peter Chernin and Steven Spielberg, many of the powerful people he turned down went to Sarandos, and Bajaria and Lin were fired two days apart.
Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos fired chief content officer Bela Bajaria on October 14 and film chief Dan Lin two days later, Lucas Shaw reported in Sunday's Bloomberg Screentime, based on conversations with more than a dozen people. US engagement had slipped, measured in qualified play days (days a month a customer watches). Shaw reports talent was the deciding issue: the Duffer Brothers, Noah Baumbach and Shawn Levy left, David Fincher did not renew his deal, and partners Lin turned down went to Sarandos. Sarandos told analysts that Peter Rice "understands talent relations." Netflix declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication: Two Netflix executives lost their jobs partly because partners Dan Lin turned down went over his head to Sarandos, and Peter Rice starts the job with a public mandate to win those filmmakers back.
The Facts
  • Sarandos told Bajaria she was fired around 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday, October 14; he dismissed Lin two days later. Peter Rice, a Disney and Fox veteran, replaced Bajaria.
  • Engagement: the average customer is spending fewer days a month watching Netflix (qualified play days) and less time on the service; the problem was most acute in the US.
  • Shows that fell short, per Shaw: Little House on the Prairie; new seasons of Beef lost most of their viewers. Netflix won its fewest Emmys in a decade.
  • Lin, brought in by Bajaria in 2024, pared the film slate and passed on ideas from partners including Peter Chernin and Steven Spielberg; "many" of the powerful people he turned down reached out to Sarandos.
  • Departures cited: the Duffer Brothers, Noah Baumbach and Shawn Levy left for other companies; David Fincher opted not to renew his deal (Shaw: he is taking a sabbatical, not leaving for a rival). The Duffers and Levy left to make theatrical films.
  • Lin's record cited by Shaw: most of his films this year rated "loved" on Netflix's internal MVS satisfaction metric; an Oscar contender three years running (Emilia Perez, Train Dreams, La Bola Negra).
  • Sarandos on the analyst call: "Peter Rice understands talent relations. In a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life."
  • Greg Peters at a staff town hall: "Two things can be true. We have an enviable, growing and profitable business. And, at the same time, we know there's more work to do to drive more growth."
  • Netflix is on pace for about $15 billion in profit this year; shares fell 6.6% last week, which Shaw attributes mainly to the year-end forecast.
  • Sarandos first approached Rice about managing the Warner Bros. assets during Netflix's bid for Warner Bros.; those talks picked up again in recent weeks.

TheWrap's Kayla Cobb reports that creators are adding live events as a revenue stream, with platforms paying to back them. Live Nation launched Creator Nation this month, led by Scott Fisher (founder of Select Management Group) and Alexis Fisher (founder of Timeline Management), to handle content, commerce, brand partnerships and live shows for creators without a touring or music agent. Patreon has run creator events since 2024 and uses some to move fans into higher-priced membership tiers. Alexis Fisher said a large following does not automatically produce hard-ticket buyers.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): Live Nation's Creator Nation decides who tours by whether a creator has already sold merch, a product or a meet-and-greet, and that sales record is now what a creator brings to a hard-ticket deal.
The Facts
  • Dude Perfect's second tour, "Squad Games," grossed $11.4 million in ticket sales this year.
  • "Anazala Family Live," the channel's first live event, sold out Newark's Prudential Center in 25 minutes; Live Nation was the only company that backed the concept, per Anas Marwah.
  • Patreon expects to host 18 creator-fan events this year, a 64% increase from a year ago; it has helped creators with live events since 2024. CMO Mike McGarry: an exclusive event can be "a motivator to encourage a fan to be part of a higher-cost tier."
  • Creator Nation (Live Nation) was announced earlier this month, led by co-founders Scott Fisher and Alexis Fisher.
  • Alexis Fisher: "There are a lot of times where creators will have huge followings on social media and a lot of likes, but that doesn't automatically make [the audience] hard ticket buyers." Her screen: "Have they ever sold merch? Have they ever sold a product? Have they ever hosted a meet and greet?"
  • Three Madison Square Garden shows by podcasters Hannah Berner and Paige DeSorbo sold out in under an hour, prompting a fourth; Salish Matter's Sincerely Yours launch drew more than 80,000 people to the American Dream Mall.
  • An NRG study with TheWrap: 49% of Gen Z women prefer real-world events to digital ones.

SAG-AFTRA's Streaming Bonus Is Paying 700 Performers $1.5 Million for 2024 Work
About 700 performers will split roughly $1.5 million from the streaming bonus fund won in 2023, about 0.4 percent of a membership above 160,000, for high-budget SVOD work released in 2024.
SAG-AFTRA told its national board this weekend that the first payout from the streaming success bonus it won in the 2023 strike will reach about 700 performers, per Deadline. A title that clears the viewership threshold pays each principal performer 100 percent of the fixed residual; the performer keeps 75 percent and 25 percent goes to a fund run by SAG-AFTRA and AMPTP trustees, with no disclosed formula for that share. Health plan eligibility still requires $28,933 a year in union earnings, and members behind on dues will be terminated at the end of October.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): The 2023 streaming bonus reached about 700 performers in its first payout, so for a working actor the value of a streaming job still sits in the fixed residual and in clearing the $28,933 health plan threshold.
The Facts
  • Roughly $1.5 million will go from the bonus distribution fund to about 700 performers for work on high-budget SVOD projects released in 2024 (SAG-AFTRA overview of the national board plenary, Monday).
  • That is about 0.4% of SAG-AFTRA's 160,000+ members; more than 100,000 members are actors and performers.
  • Bonus mechanics: a title over the viewership threshold triggers a payment to each principal performer equal to 100% of the fixed residual; the performer receives 75%, and 25% goes to a fund controlled by SAG-AFTRA and AMPTP trustees for distribution to other members. No details yet on how the 25% is distributed or whether it is included in Monday's figures.
  • Health plan: qualifying requires $28,933 in annual union-contracted income; SAG-AFTRA agreed to deep plan cuts earlier this year in exchange for a health fund infusion.
  • SAG-AFTRA returns to its regular membership policy at the end of October: members not current on dues will be terminated.
  • Sean Astin (president), in a 12-minute video: "Cable and then streaming steadily dismantled that system, and we've spent years fighting to reclaim it. What we've won back is substantial, but it's nowhere near what it was."
  • Drake Bell, Cecily Strong, Jack Haven and Heather Matarazzo have publicly described losing or nearly losing coverage; Cheyenne Jackson launched "ONE JOB AWAY" to spotlight actors close to qualifying and reports "hundreds" of submissions.

Microdrama Apps Are Spending Half Their Revenue to Find Viewers
The 16 leading vertical apps outside China released 32,000 titles in the third quarter, PineDrama alone 15,501, and Tommy Harper's VeYou shuts its standalone app on November 6.
The Ankler's Elaine Low reports a shakeout forming in microdramas. Owl & Co. founder Hernan Lopez says most apps spend 50 percent or more of revenue on customer acquisition. Holywater co-CEO Bogdan Nesvit says his My Drama app gets 70 percent of new users through paid marketing and that other platforms run as high as 90 percent. In China, 91 percent of third-quarter releases were AI-generated.

  • Holywater (My Drama): 70% of new users acquired through paid means, 30% organic; runs about 50,000 unique video trailers a month on TikTok, Instagram and other channels; other platforms' paid share can reach 90% (Bogdan Nesvit).

  • Holywater deals: Fox (around 200 vertical series), Dhar Mann's studio, Kevin Hart's Hartbeat.

  • China: 91% of Q3 microdrama releases were AI-generated (Owl & Co.); Lopez says the U.S. trails China by about 18 to 24 months and fewer than 20% of Americans watch a vertical app monthly.
  • Top four genres = 64% of viewing: hidden identity 30%, romance 17%, revenge 16%, billionaire/CEO 10%.
  • ReelShort live-action titles were more likely than AI titles to stay in the app's top 10 over 30 days (Owl & Co.). Nesvit: "You still need script writers to produce AI movies... We've tried creating scripts with AI. It doesn't work."

Elvis Presley's Catalog Owners Are Suing Anthropic for $41 Million Over 274 Songs
Authentic Brands Group and other Presley rights holders sued Anthropic on October 23, claiming Claude was trained on 274 Presley songs without permission and seeking about $150,000 per song.
Authentic Brands Group, which owns rights to Elvis Presley's music, filed a copyright suit against Anthropic on October 23 with other Presley rights holders, Pitchfork reported after viewing the filing. The suit says Anthropic trained Claude on 274 Presley songs, including "Can't Help Falling in Love," and that Claude still produces close copies. It seeks roughly $150,000 per song, about $41 million. Anthropic told Pitchfork it disagrees and will defend the case. Major labels and publishers have sued Anthropic before; Pitchfork called this one of the first such suits by the owner of a single artist's catalog.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The Presley owners are asking $150,000 a song on 274 songs, and an artist or estate that owns its catalog outright can bring that claim itself, without a label or publisher in the lead.
The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: Authentic Brands Group (Tennessee-based, per Pitchfork) and co-plaintiffs holding Presley rights.
  • Defendant: Anthropic. Filed October 23, 2026; viewed by Pitchfork.
  • Claim: Claude trained on 274 Presley songs without permission; songs named include "Can't Help Falling in Love," "Don't Be Cruel," "Farther Along," "If You Think I Don't Need You," "Run On." The suit also alleges "unlicensed derivative works."
  • Damages sought: about $150,000 per song, about $41M total.
  • Filing, quoting Claude: "These renders keep landing very close to the originals: same structure, same hooks reused with light rewording..."
  • Lead attorney Richard Busch: the defendant "has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before."
  • Anthropic to Pitchfork: "We disagree with the claims and intend to defend this case fully."
  • Pitchfork: major labels and music publishers have filed claims against Anthropic before; this is one of the first high-profile cases by the owner of a single artist's catalog.

Doug Shapiro Expects AI to Make Quality Content Abundant and Weaken Its Pricing Power
In a new essay, Shapiro argues flat consumer attention plus falling AI production costs will bring more quality content, lower hit rates, creators taking share and weaker pricing for content itself.
Doug Shapiro published part one of a two-part series on Sunday arguing that two facts are reliable enough to plan on: consumer attention is not growing, and generative AI will sharply cut creation costs. From those he predicts more quality content, more substitutable hits, lower hit rates, creators taking share and weaker pricing power for content. He expects value to move to whoever creates demand for specific content, controls the moment of consumer choice, or sells complementary products. His Morgan Stanley-based chart shows platforms such as Netflix and YouTube took almost all media value from 2018 to 2025.
Potential Talent Implication: In Shapiro's read the work itself becomes easier to replace, and what keeps its price for talent is an audience that asks for them by name plus a share of the products and services sold around the work.
The Facts
  • Title: "The Predictable Economic Consequences of Infinite Content" (part one of two; part two will cover implications for a media company). Paid post with a partial free preview.
  • Two premises Shapiro calls highly confident: "consumer attention isn't really growing and GenAI will dramatically reduce creation costs."
  • Predicted consequences: "quality content supply will explode; even high-quality content will become more substitutable; hit rates will fall; creators will take share; content pricing power will weaken; and for a lot of content, monetization will move from the content itself to complementary products and services."
  • Where value shifts: "creating differentiated demand," "coordinating demand (controlling the moment of consumer choice)," and "monetizing complements."
  • Biggest unknown, per Shapiro: who controls coordination, and whether GenAI uncouples coordination from distribution.
  • Figure 1 (source: Morgan Stanley, The Mediator): from 2018 to 2025, essentially all value created in media accrued to digital consumer platforms (Meta, Netflix, Spotify, YouTube, TikTok, Valve/Steam, Roku).

The BBC Has Found Only £200 Million of the £500 Million It Must Cut by 2028
Closing BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra in spring 2027 saves about £10 million, two insiders told Deadline; the BBC has announced about 1,200 of a planned 2,000 job cuts.
The BBC must save £500 million ($670 million) by 2028 after losing more than two million licence fee payers since 2020, and it has announced £200 million of that so far, Deadline reported Saturday. Director general Matt Brittin announced the three channel closures on Tuesday. BBC leaders also discussed merging children's channels CBBC and CBeebies and folding BBC Sounds into iPlayer. Funding talks with the government, which include a proposed "Netflix tax" (a surcharge on streaming subscriptions), leave the BBC with no view of its finances past the end of 2027.
Potential Talent Implication: The BBC has promised more spending on younger audiences without naming a figure, and until its funding settlement lands, UK producers pitching comedy and youth series are selling to a buyer that cannot see past 2027.
The Facts
  • Savings target: £500 million ($670 million) by 2028; £200 million announced to date.
  • Licence fee payers lost since 2020: more than two million. Public income: £3.9 billion.
  • Closures announced Tuesday, October 20: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra, switching off in spring 2027; estimated saving about £10 million (two insiders).
  • Job cuts announced: about 1,200, which Deadline put at 800 short of the target. BBC workforce down 10% since 2020.
  • BBC Media Tech must save £102 million by next year; BBC News contributes at least £51 million.
  • Discussed and rejected: merging CBBC with CBeebies. Discussed, no decision: folding BBC Sounds into iPlayer.
  • Recently cancelled on BBC Three: RuPaul's Drag Race UK, The Rap Game, I Kissed a Girl/Boy.

Hello Sunshine Sold for Under 10 Percent of Its 2021 Price, and Investors Have Moved to Creators
Candle Media valued Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine at $900 million in 2021 and is selling it back for far less than 10 percent of that, while Kevin Hart has already bought out his own private equity investor.
The Ankler's Ashley Cullins tallies the early-2020s star company deals. Candle bought a majority of Hello Sunshine at a $900 million valuation and is selling it to Witherspoon and Mediawan for far less than 10 percent of that. Candle's 2022 stake valued Will Smith's Westbrook at $600 million, and Abry valued Hartbeat at about $650 million before Hart reportedly bought Abry out with Authentic Brands money. Investor Ed Simpson says the money now buys "audiences it can measure and libraries it can own," and TPG and The Chernin Group are looking at creators.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): The 2021 prices were paid for a development slate and a famous name; the investors still writing checks want a library the company owns and an audience it can measure, and most star companies that sell their shows to studios own neither.
The Facts
  • Hello Sunshine: Candle Media (backed by Blackstone, led by Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs) took a majority stake in August 2021 at a $900 million valuation; Witherspoon is buying it back with Mediawan for "far less than 10 percent of that number."
  • Mayer, to Semafor: Hello Sunshine is "still profitable, not terrible, but it wasn't worth what we paid."
  • Westbrook (Will Smith): Candle reportedly invested $60 million for 10 percent in January 2022 ($600 million valuation); restructured in 2024; this month announced a slate partnership with The Malar Group including 215, a scripted series about Smith's early music career. Candle still holds its stake.
  • Hartbeat (Kevin Hart): Abry Partners invested $100 million in April 2022 at about a $650 million valuation for 15 percent; in early 2026 Hart announced an Authentic Brands Group partnership and reportedly used the cash to buy back Abry's stake. Hartbeat this month signed a vertical drama first-look with Fox Entertainment.

  • Plan B (Brad Pitt): Mediawan bought a majority stake valuing it around $300 million in December 2022.
  • Mediawan (KKR-backed) owns nearly 100 labels, including Plan B, See-Saw Films, Kinetic Content and Peter Chernin's North Road Company.
  • Companies without private equity: LuckyChap, Monkeypaw, Blossom Films, Brownstone Productions; they rely on first-look or overall deals to cover overhead.
  • Ed Simpson: "In the early 2020s, Hollywood deals in general were paying for people, and now the smart money is buying audiences it can measure and libraries it can own."

Artists Equity's Indie Label Gives the Creative Team Half the Points and Sits Outside Its Netflix and Sony Deals
Amy Baer told IndieWire that AEIP films fall below the minimum budgets in Artists Equity's Netflix and Sony output deals, so they are free to sell elsewhere, and still carry streaming viewership bonuses.
Amy Baer, president of film and television at Ben Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity, said its new label, Artists Equity Independent Pictures, runs on the company's model: talent takes a smaller fee up front and equity in the film. In a typical indie, she said, half the points go to the filmmaking team and half to financiers; AEIP hands the creative team its half to divide. Because AEIP budgets sit below the minimums in the Netflix streaming and Sony Pictures theatrical output deals, those deals do not bind the label, though either buyer can still acquire a film.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): An AEIP film pays less up front, but the creative team holds half the points and the film can sell to any buyer, which puts the value in how the points are split and what the film sells for.
The Facts
  • Label: Artists Equity Independent Pictures (AEIP), led by Jennifer Westin (formerly physical production at Topic Studios), reporting to Baer.
  • Model (Baer): "In a typical indie film, 50 percent of the points go to the filmmaking team, the other 50 percent go to the financiers. We just say to the creative team, 'Here's your points. Carve it up.' We're not going to tell you how to do it."
  • Output deals: Artists Equity has Netflix (streaming) and Sony Pictures (theatrical) output deals with minimum budget levels; AEIP films will typically fall beneath them and are not bound by either; Netflix or Sony can still buy one.
  • Bonuses: AEIP films still qualify for performance bonuses at streaming viewership thresholds, as on The Rip, where Artists Equity paid a percentage of salary to each of 1,200 crew members; thresholds and amounts undisclosed ("robust" views, "substantial" bonus).
  • First titles: A Woman in the Sun (writer-director Julia Cox; Renée Zellweger, Sissy Spacek, Mia Threapleton; Black Bear distributing) and Downriver (director Sam Jones; Garrett Hedlund, Jake Lacy, Jessica Biel).
  • Sourcing: packaged projects, not internal development; no low-budget slasher horror or experimental films.
  • Baer: "This is not a talent production company on steroids."

  • Callif example: a film Paramount Skydance was initially "bullish about moving full steam ahead" on; its prospects at the company died about two weeks ago.

Agencies Want Producers to Get Their Shows Back From Streamers After Three Years
The American Entertainment Alliance would cap streamer exclusivity at three years for films and five years for series, and UTA's Rich Shuter told Puck that license fees would fall.
Puck laid out the terms of the American Entertainment Alliance plan to revive fin-syn (the old rules limiting network ownership of outside shows). Streamers with at least 10 million U.S. subscribers would spend half of original film and series budgets, excluding sports and library, with independent producers. Exclusive rights would end after three years for films; for series, two years after the third season airs, capped at five years after the first-season finale. The original streamer gets first negotiation on an extension but no right to match. The coalition has hired Akin Gump to lobby Congress.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The plan swaps the up-front premium for a second sale: UTA's Rich Shuter concedes streamers would pay lower license fees, and in return the producer gets the show back after three years with a library to license again.
The Facts
  • Coalition: CAA, WME, UTA, Ziffren Brittenham, Blumhouse, Imagine and Legendary among members; registered months ago at CAA's Century City address; public debut in the New York Times and on The Town.
  • Scope: streamers with at least 10 million U.S. subscribers; half of spending on original films and series, excluding sports and library acquisitions, to independent producers (companies neither owning nor affiliated with a qualifying streamer).
  • Exclusivity caps: films three years; television two years after the third season airs, outer limit five years after the first-season finale (Shuter's suggestion).
  • Extension: first negotiation right for the original streamer, no matching right.
  • Lobbying: Akin Gump retained (Lauren Rubin, Democrat; Geoff Verhoff, Republican). Pursued as separate legislation from the pending bipartisan production tax credit bill.
  • Shuter acknowledged to Puck that streamers would pay lower license fees under the plan.
  • Gardner's open questions: which agency administers it (F.C.C. or F.T.C.), who audits the 50 percent, and First Amendment exposure; cites Schurz Communications v. F.C.C. (7th Cir. 1992).

California's Tax Credit Now Backs 40 Percent of LA Location Shoots, and Production Is Still Falling
FilmLA counted 4,171 on-location shoot days in Los Angeles from July through September, down 4.8 percent from a year earlier, while credit-backed projects reached a record 40.3 percent of scripted location work.
FilmLA's quarterly report shows California's expanded credit, raised to $750 million a year from $330 million, now funds 62 percent of TV comedy and 49.4 percent of TV drama location days, up from about 20 percent each a year ago. Total shoot days are still 36 percent below the five-year average, per The Hollywood Reporter. Features rose 2.1 percent to 533 days; commercials, which the credit does not cover, fell 15.9 percent. Mayor Karen Bass called for an uncapped credit and a federal one. The program still does not count above-the-line costs.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Above-the-line pay still does not qualify for California's credit, so on a California show the subsidy covers crew and production costs while the talent fee is the part of the budget the producer pays in full.
The Facts
  • Q3 2026 (July to September): 4,171 on-location shoot days, down 4.8 percent year over year (Deadline); down about 11 percent from Q2 and 36 percent below the five-year average (THR). Q2 decline was 13 percent.
  • Credit share: incentivized projects 40.3 percent of scripted on-location production, nearly double a year ago.
  • TV: credit-backed projects 62 percent of TV comedy and 49.4 percent of TV drama shoot days (19 percent and 20.6 percent a year ago). THR: TV 1,400 days, down about 3 percent; drama 494 days, down 9 percent; comedy 192 days, up 143 percent.
  • Features: 533 days, up 2.1 percent; incentivized 24.4 percent, mostly independents; studio titles include 13 Going on 30 (Netflix), Cut Off (Warner Bros.), They Follow (Neon).
  • Commercials: 562 days, down 15.9 percent; not eligible for the credit; more than 41 percent below the five-year average.
  • Program: annual cap raised to $750 million from $330 million in 2025; 214 projects selected since July 2025.
  • FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches: "Overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be."
  • Mayor Karen Bass called for "an uncapped California film and television tax credit" and a federal credit.
  • ProdPro: New York production spend up 87 percent in the quarter vs. California's 17 percent.
  • THR: the open question is whether California will let above-the-line costs qualify, as most regions with credits do.

Senior Streaming Executives Leave Faster Than Studio Executives, a Count of 1,387 Appointments Finds
Stephen Follows counted 1,387 senior appointments since 2011: 17 percent of streaming appointees left within two years against 11 percent at studios, and 31 percent against 21 percent by year three.
Stephen Follows, a data analyst, pulled 11,802 trade stories from nine publications since January 2011 and tracked 531 senior appointments at streamers and 856 at studios. At the very top layer, a quarter of streaming chiefs left within two years against 14 percent at studios. HBO Max lost 30 percent of senior appointees within two years and Paramount+ 26 percent, while Netflix lost 15 percent and Amazon Prime Video 18 percent. Of 185 reported streaming exits, 22 percent used words of removal and 30 percent came with a restructure or a new boss.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Streaming executives leave faster than studio executives, and one in 12 reported exits mentioned a production or first-look deal, so the executive who ordered a project may be gone, or across the table as a producer, before it is delivered.
The Facts
  • 1,387 senior appointments tracked: 531 at seven streamers and 856 at traditional studios; 11,802 articles from nine publications, January 2011 to the start of October 2026.
  • Left within two years: 17 percent at streamers, 11 percent at studios; within three years 31 versus 21 percent; within five years 51 versus 36 percent.
  • Top layer (chiefs, chairs, presidents, heads of film, television, content and marketing): 247 streaming and 362 studio appointments; a quarter of streaming executives gone within two years against 14 percent at studios; half gone within four and a half years at streamers and six at studios.
  • Within two years: HBO Max 30 percent, Paramount+ 26 percent, Amazon Prime Video 18 percent, Netflix 15 percent; half of Netflix appointees were still in post after six years; at Disney half were still in post after 13 years.
  • Of 185 reported senior streaming exits: 22 percent removal words, 30 percent restructure or new boss, 26 percent another job, 4 percent leaving to start a company or produce, 2 percent retirement or personal, 16 percent no reason cited.
  • One in 12 streaming exit stories mentioned a production or first-look deal.

SAG-AFTRA's Microdrama Agreement Pays Leads $250 a Day on Budgets Capped at $300,000
A year after SAG-AFTRA's Verticals Agreement, dozens of microdramas are union-covered: leads get a $250 minimum for eight hours, budgets cap at $300,000, and shoots run no longer than 30 consecutive days.
TheWrap reports that SAG-AFTRA's independent Verticals Agreement, which covers vertical microdramas (short serialized video made for phones), turned one last week. The union says it has signed off on dozens of productions out of hundreds made each year. Leads receive a minimum of $250 for an eight-hour day and $468.75 for 12 hours, against a $1,246 baseline for a television day player. Producers pay pension and health contributions for every performer, union or not. Actor JT Garcia went from $600 a day on ReelShort productions to more than $1,200 a day plus 20 percent.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): The $250 lead minimum sits below what some leads are paid: JT Garcia went from $600 to more than $1,200 a day plus 20 percent, with pension and health contributions paid by the producer on top.
The Facts
  • Budget cap $300,000; most microdramas cost $150,000 to $300,000; shooting limited to 30 consecutive days.
  • Lead minimum: $250 for eight hours, $468.75 for 12 hours. Non-lead minimum: $164 for eight hours, $307.50 for 12 hours. Television day-player baseline under the 2026 television agreement: $1,246.
  • Overtime: 1.5 times after eight hours for hours nine and 10, double time from hour 11.
  • A nonmember who works one principal role on a covered vertical can use it to seek union membership.
  • Productions named: Knockout Shorts (five SAG productions), Snow Story Productions (hundreds of verticals, three union), Issa Rae's "Screentime" (TikTok and Pine Drama), Taye Diggs' "Tides of Temptation" (with Lifetime and Microhouse Films).

Screen International reports that A Woman Asleep, by artist and director Vikki Bardot, is one of 10 films in the main competition at FilmFestival Cottbus in Germany, November 3 to 8. Studios Want AI-Made Franchises but Cannot Copyright What AI Makes Alone
Arcos Labs founder Nelson Chu says several dozen studio executives want to make IP with AI, and his VN Studio logs which steps humans performed to support a copyright claim.
Under US copyright rules, purely AI-generated material generally cannot be copyrighted, which blocks studios from owning characters and franchises made that way. Nelson Chu, whose six-person startup Arcos Labs spoke with several dozen studio executives over months, says they want to stop others from generating their IP while generating their own with AI. Arcos's VN Studio, shown first to The Ankler, records which actions were done by AI and which by humans and screens for third-party IP. Chu does not guarantee a copyright, and the legal questions remain unsettled.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A studio cannot copyright what AI makes alone, so on an AI-assisted project the human work that writers, directors and artists can document could be the part that carries ownership.
The Facts
  • Source: The Ankler, Ashley Cullins, October 16, 2026, in the Dealmakers section.
  • Rule: purely AI-generated material generally cannot be copyrighted under US rules; only original works created by humans are eligible.
  • Arcos Labs: a six-person startup founded by Nelson Chu, who previously raised $50 million for the private credit startup Percent. It soft-launched this year and debuted VN in August, which it calls a fidelity recognition engine that measures how closely AI content resembles protected IP and human likenesses.
  • VN Studio: a new production platform revealed exclusively to The Ankler. It logs which actions were executed by AI and which by humans, and screens for recognizable third-party IP introduced during production. Chu will not guarantee copyright.
  • Chu: "They don't want anyone else to be able to generate their IP," describing several dozen studio executives, who added "But wait, I want to be able to generate my IP using AI."
  • A lawyer who advises studios and production companies said every studio general counsel would "fall all over themselves" for an easy tool that solves this, and that VN Studio could be "extremely pivotal" if it works as Chu describes.
  • The article notes the legal system may not give studios exclusive rights to all AI-assisted creations.

Netflix Puts Producer Peter Rice in Charge of All Its Content
Netflix is replacing chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice, starting October 26, a day after laying off about 1,000 employees and five days before its third-quarter earnings.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos told Bajaria late Wednesday that she was being replaced, according to The Ankler. Netflix announced Thursday that Rice, a former chairman of Walt Disney Television who now produces films, will oversee scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Puck, which broke the news, reports that film chief Dan Lin is expected to leave and that the decision belongs to Rice. Netflix engagement rose 2 percent in the first half of 2026 and its shares are down more than 40 percent in a year. The Facts

CAA, WME and UTA Are Lobbying to Require Half of Streamer Content Budgets Go to Independent Producers
The American Entertainment Alliance, with CAA, WME, UTA, Blumhouse, Imagine and Legendary as founding members, wants a law requiring big studios and streamers to put half of original content budgets into independent projects.
The American Entertainment Alliance launched October 15 with CAA, WME and UTA among its founding members, alongside producers including Jason Blum, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer. It wants Congress to require companies such as Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Skydance to spend half of their original content budgets on independent U.S. shows and movies made by non-studio entities. The proposal resembles the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules (Fin-Syn, which restricted network ownership of programming until the 1990s repeal). The New York Times first reported the group and says the companies are likely to fight any bill.
Potential Talent Implication: Under the proposal, a producer with a show outside the studio system would be selling into a pool of buyer money reserved by law, and the Times reports top producers could see bigger paydays.
The Facts
  • The group is called the American Entertainment Alliance (AEA). TheWrap says the New York Times reported it first; Deadline carries the same news the same day.
  • Deadline lists the founding members as CAA, WME, UTA, Anonymous Content, Blumhouse, Imagine Entertainment, Jeff Sagansky, Legendary Entertainment, MRC, North Road, Producers United, Propagate Content and Ziffren Brittenham.
  • TheWrap names producers Jason Blum, Peter Chernin, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer as supporters.
  • The ask is bipartisan legislation requiring major studios and streamers to devote half of their original content budgets to independent shows and movies produced in the United States by non-studio entities.
  • Companies named as targets: Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Skydance.
  • Fin-Syn limited network ownership of programming in the 1970s and 1980s and was repealed in the 1990s; series such as Hill Street Blues, The Mary Tyler Moore Show, Seinfeld and Roseanne were independently produced.
  • CAA chief Bryan Lourd: "There are fewer people deciding what gets made and what we all see, what the consumer sees... Distribution is not the issue of the future. Who finances content is the issue."
  • UTA Vice Chair Jay Sures: "As film and television increasingly consolidate, we need a regulatory framework that puts creators first, protects industry workers and preserves competition."
  • The Times says the companies have large Washington lobbying operations and will argue they already buy plenty of programming from outside studios.

Netflix Cuts 1,000 Jobs While Saying Its Business Is Strong
Netflix cut about 6% of its global staff, roughly 1,000 jobs, on Wednesday in its largest layoff since 2022, with product, tech, legal and HR teams hit hardest.
Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters told employees in a memo, which Deadline obtained, that the business is strong and on track for its full-year forecast, and that Netflix will keep investing aggressively in high-impact areas. Deadline reports the stock is down more than 40% over the past year to just under $70 against a 52-week high of $125, and viewer engagement rose only 2% in the first half of the year to 97 billion hours. Netflix reports third-quarter earnings on October 20.
Potential Talent Implication: Netflix says it will keep investing aggressively in high-impact areas, and with its stock down more than 40% in a year, the work most likely to get paid for is work that moves engagement.
The Facts
  • About 6% of Netflix's global staff, some 1,000 jobs, cut Wednesday; the largest round in four years. Greatest impact: product, tech, legal and HR.
  • Memo from Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters: "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast."
  • Stock just under $70, down more than 40% over the past year and 25% year to date; 52-week high $125.
  • Engagement up 2% in the first half of 2026 to 97 billion hours viewed. Sarandos at a Bloomberg conference: "Overall, we're not growing as fast as I want us to."
  • Q2 revenue $12.6 billion (up 13%), operating margin 33%. Q3 earnings October 20.
  • Strategy shifts named: live events and sports, video podcasts, creator-driven content, and theatrical releases.

Skydance Shares Fall 25% as It Issues 471 Million Warrants to Paramount Shareholders
Skydance stock fell as much as 25% to $6.78 on Wednesday as the company distributed about 471 million warrants letting Paramount Skydance Class B holders buy shares at $12.
Skydance, formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, began trading October 6 under SKYD with a market value of about $34 billion. If every warrant were exercised the company would raise about $5.65 billion and dilute current holders. Variety reports pro forma revenue near $70 billion and almost $80 billion in net debt. Wells Fargo analysts led by Steven Cahall, who rate the stock underweight with a $7 target, said they expect Skydance to deliver its planned $6 billion in cost synergies and named integration leakage as the main risk.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): Skydance carries almost $80 billion in net debt and plans about $6 billion in cost savings, and while that plan is carried out, talent negotiating there may find guaranteed money easier to get than contingent upside.
The Facts
  • SKYD fell as much as 25.4% to $6.78 as of 11 a.m. ET; market cap about $34 billion; trading since October 6.
  • About 471 million warrants distributed to holders of PSKY Class B shares; each buys one Skydance share at $12, the price paid by the $47 billion equity syndicate (Ellisons, RedBird, LionTree, Saudi, Qatari and Abu Dhabi sovereign funds).
  • Full exercise would raise about $5.65 billion. NYSE adjusted the prior close from about $9.27 to about $9.07 (warrant close $2.20).
  • Pro forma annual revenue nearly $70 billion; net debt almost $80 billion. Deal value $111 billion including WBD debt.
  • Wells Fargo (Cahall): the distribution "marks the final step in the WBD transaction closing process"; underweight, $7 target; expects ~$6 billion synergies delivered.

Lesley Goldberg reports that executives have grown risk averse since the peak TV bubble burst in 2023, that straight-to-series orders have replaced pilots, and that Comedy Central and TBS no longer serve as places to build new comedy talent. Streaming comedies run 10 or fewer episodes and often return more than a year later. Apple's "Widow's Bay," from first-time showrunner Katie Dippold, won a record 14 Emmys for a comedy series after a straight-to-series order. Paramount+ and HBO Max had largely stopped buying scripted comedies before the merger because CBS and HBO feed them.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): One rep is moving comedy writers into one-hour drama so they can sell as creators who toggle between tones, because the comedy orders that remain go mostly to a short list of proven names.
The Facts
  • Comedies were 37 percent of U.S.-produced scripted series in 2018; the count fell from 210 in 2021 to 122 in 2025.

  • "Widow's Bay" received a straight-to-series order at Apple TV after FX offered development; it set a record with 14 comedy series Emmys.
  • FX's "Adults" season two viewership rose 40 percent; John Landgraf is still investing in original comedies.

  • One rep is encouraging some writers to pivot into drama to show they can work across genres.

Disney Will Pay $20 Million for a License to Character.AI's Technology After Hiring Its CEO
Disney agreed before Character.AI's Chapter 11 filing to pay $20 million for a non-exclusive perpetual license to select Character.AI intellectual property, a month after naming the startup's former CEO its chief technology officer.
Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 in Delaware to sell substantially all of its assets, and Disney is the stalking-horse bidder (the opening bid other buyers can top). Disney would pay $20 million for a non-exclusive perpetual license of select intellectual property and company claims, and provide transition resources. Disney named former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand its first chief technology officer in September, and he reports to CEO Josh D'Amaro. Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Disney is bringing the technology for talking to its characters in house, so the voice and performance rights behind those characters may matter more in contracts than they did when a third party ran the chatbot.
The Facts
  • Price and structure: $20 million for a non-exclusive perpetual license of select IP and company claims; Disney is the stalking-horse bidder, subject to higher or better offers.
  • Filing: Character.AI filed Chapter 11 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware; the platform keeps operating during the sale.
  • Timeline: sale process aimed to conclude late November or early December.

Cruise Is Paid on Digger Revenue Before Warner Recoups a Dollar
Digger fell 60% in its second weekend to $14.4 million domestic and $35.3 million worldwide, and Variety's sources put Warner Bros.' theatrical loss at $245 million.
Variety reports, citing knowledgeable sources, that Digger, the Tom Cruise and Alejandro González Iñárritu satire, is tracking to lose $245 million in theaters. It opened to $8 million domestic last weekend, then fell 60% to $14.4 million domestic and $35.3 million worldwide, and is expected to end near $50 million globally. Variety puts break-even at $350 million; a Warner spokesperson said $300 million. The budget rose from $125 million to between $160 million and $180 million, with about $100 million more in marketing. Cruise's deal pays him a percentage of revenue before the studio recoups costs.

  • Second weekend decline: 60%. Cumulative: $14.4 million domestic, $35.3 million worldwide. Opening weekend: $8 million domestic, $20 million global.
  • Projected final: roughly $50 million worldwide. Break-even: $350 million (Variety), $300 million (Warner spokesperson).
  • Budget: greenlit at $125 million, rose to $160 million to $180 million. Global marketing about $100 million. Neither figure includes awards spend; an Oscar campaign for a film like this would run around $15 million and may be scaled back.
  • Cruise's deal pays a percentage of revenues before the studio recoups costs, so profitability takes longer.
  • Digger is Warner Bros.' last standalone release before the Paramount merger. Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy left the company the Friday it opened. No Warner film in 2026 has crossed $100 million domestic.

Royal Mail admitted its 2025 Christmas ad used an AI narrator built on ElevenLabs technology; a University of York phonetics professor found considerable similarity to Paul Vaughan, who died in 2014.

Amazon MGM Gives Jac Schaeffer a New Stargate Series After Dropping the Ordered One
Amazon MGM Studios is developing a new Stargate series with WandaVision creator Jac Schaeffer under her overall deal, after Prime Video dropped Martin Gero's ordered Stargate series in June.
Deadline reports, citing sources, that Amazon MGM Studios is developing a new Stargate series with Jac Schaeffer, the WandaVision creator, under her overall deal with the studio, with Joby Harold and Tory Tunnell executive producing and a writers room open in New York. It is the second attempt: Prime Video ordered a Stargate reboot from Martin Gero in November 2025, but in June the project was revealed as not moving forward after a 20-week writers room and pre-production in the U.K. Amazon declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Martin Gero had a series order, a 20-week writers room and U.K. pre-production on Stargate, and Amazon still dropped it, while Jac Schaeffer now holds the franchise through her overall deal.
The Facts
  • Project: new Stargate series in development at Amazon MGM Studios, led by Jac Schaeffer (WandaVision) under her overall deal. Executive producers: Schaeffer, Joby Harold, Tory Tunnell. Writers room opened in New York. Amazon declined comment. Variety reported it first.
  • Prior attempt: reboot from Martin Gero received a Prime Video series order in November 2025; in June it was revealed it would not move forward, after a 20-week writers room and while in pre-production in the U.K.
  • Franchise: began with the 1994 feature by Roland Emmerich and Dean Devlin; SG-1 (1997 to 2007), Atlantis (2004 to 2009), Universe (2009 to 2011), animated Infinity (2002 to 2003).
  • Amazon's $8.5 billion MGM acquisition in 2022 identified Stargate among the first MGM titles for adaptations.

NBC Fires Co-Creator Gail Lerner From Newlyweds Two Weeks Before Its Premiere
NBC let go of co-creator Gail Lerner from Newlyweds on Friday for creative differences, after six episodes were made under her leadership; the sitcom premieres October 23.
NBC removed Gail Lerner, co-creator of the sitcom Newlyweds, on Friday, and an NBC spokesperson confirmed that creative differences led to her exit. Lerner said on Instagram that the first six episodes were made under her leadership. The show has finished several episodes, with episode 8 filming, and a planned hiatus next week will be used to find a new showrunner. Co-creator Jamie Lee Curtis, who is also an executive producer and recurring star, stays. The premiere on October 23 is unaffected.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): A co-creator who ran the room for the first six episodes was removed for creative differences two weeks before the premiere, while the other co-creator, who is also an executive producer and a recurring star, stays.
The Facts
  • Exit: Lerner let go Friday, Oct. 9; reason given to her and confirmed by NBC: creative differences. NBC declined further comment.
  • Status: several episodes finished; episode 8 filming in Los Angeles; hiatus planned next week to be used to find a new showrunner; Oct. 23 premiere on NBC unchanged.
  • Cast: Téa Leoni and Tim Daly (a real-life married couple), Emma Meisel, Ignacio Diaz-Silverio, Bill O'Neill; Jamie Lee Curtis plays Daly's ex-wife.
  • Lerner on Instagram: "The first six episodes were made under my leadership, and I wouldn't change a thing."
  • Curtis created the show with Lerner and has pushed for multi-cam sitcoms on free broadcast television.

Joe Rogan Dropped Spotify Exclusivity in 2024 and Still Renewed for a Reported $250 Million
Spotify renewed The Joe Rogan Experience on a multiyear license covering ad sales and licensing while the show stays on YouTube and Apple; The Wall Street Journal reported an estimated $250 million earnout.
Spotify and Joe Rogan signed a new multiyear licensing agreement on Oct. 8, extending a relationship that began in 2020. Spotify keeps handling ad sales and licensing for The Joe Rogan Experience, which runs on several services; Rogan ended his Spotify exclusivity in 2024. Terms were not disclosed. Variety, citing anonymous sources in The Wall Street Journal, reports the deal resembles the 2024 agreement and carries an estimated earnout (payments earned over the term) of $250 million. It ranked as the most-listened-to podcast on Spotify, YouTube and Apple Podcasts in 2025.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Rogan gave up Spotify exclusivity two years ago, kept the show on YouTube and Apple, and Spotify still renewed for a reported $250 million to sell his ads and license the show.
The Facts
  • Deal: new multiyear licensing agreement, announced Oct. 8, 2026. Spotify continues to handle ad sales and licensing for The Joe Rogan Experience, which is available across multiple services.
  • Terms not disclosed. Per The Wall Street Journal (anonymous sources, via Variety): similar to the early-2024 deal, with "an estimated earnout of $250 million" over the term.
  • History: show came to Spotify in September 2020 and later became exclusive; Rogan ended exclusivity in 2024.
  • Rogan: "The partnership with Spotify has been an amazing fit... I'm extremely happy and excited to continue with them for years to come."
  • Jordan Newman, head of content partnerships, Spotify: "Joe has built something incredibly enduring..."
  • Scale: No. 1 most-listened-to podcast on Spotify, YouTube and Apple Podcasts in 2025; 18 million Spotify followers; more than 2,500 episodes since December 2009.

Artists Equity Pays Its Writers, Directors and Actors Like Equity Investors, and Netflix Shares the Data
Ben Affleck told Variety that Artists Equity shares all streaming revenue with writers, directors, actors and producers on top of fees, and negotiated Netflix bonuses that pay a film's entire crew.
In a Variety cover interview published Oct. 7, Ben Affleck described how Artists Equity, formed in 2022 by Affleck, Matt Damon and RedBird Capital's Gerry Cardinale, pays talent. Writers, directors, actors and producers are "compensated exactly as equity financiers would be," Affleck said. Variety reports the company shares all streaming revenue with them in addition to fees, and negotiated performance bonuses with Netflix that pay a film's entire crew. Affleck said Netflix agreed to share information on what succeeds on its platform, that the model began with Air at Amazon, and that "People got bonuses."
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Affleck and Damon got Netflix to share its performance data and pay bonuses off it, which gives any producer with a Netflix deal a precedent for asking who sees the numbers behind a bonus.
The Facts
  • Artists Equity: founded 2022 by Ben Affleck and Matt Damon with RedBird Capital's Gerry Cardinale; Variety calls it the leading outside producer of Netflix original films (first-look deal to produce films for the service). Netflix acquired Affleck's AI startup InterPositive in July for nearly $590 million in cash.
  • Model (Variety): shares all streaming revenue with above-the-line talent (screenwriters, directors, actors, producers) in addition to traditional fees; negotiated performance-based bonuses with Netflix that pay the entire crew of a film.
  • Affleck: "We seek to compensate old-school above the line talent... as if they were investors in a film. It works on the clean, evident construction that those parties are compensated exactly as equity financiers would be. Not in some kind of arcane, separate bonus pool."
  • Affleck: "Netflix was willing to share some information about what's successful on their platform." "We've had success. People got bonuses."
  • Origin: started with Air at Amazon; The Rip at Netflix cited as another example. Partnerships named: Netflix and Sony.
  • Also: Artists Equity Independent Pictures, an indie theatrical film fund for next-generation filmmakers (filed 10/7). Next release: Animals (Affleck directs and stars; Kerry Washington, Steven Yeun, Gillian Anderson).

Xbox Now Runs Its Own Film, Merchandise and Theme Park Business for Minecraft, Halo and Call of Duty
Xbox formed XP under Mojang president Kayleen Walters, an executive producer of A Minecraft Movie, to run film and TV, licensing, sponsorships and live events for its game franchises.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced XP on Oct. 8, a division with four units: Xbox Pictures for film and TV adaptations, Xbox Products for licensing and merchandise, Xbox Partnerships for sponsors and Xbox Places for events, theme parks and location-based experiences. Kayleen Walters leads it; she spent 13 years at Lucasfilm, grew Minecraft consumer products to more than 250 licensees, and produced A Minecraft Movie and its sequel. The franchises include Minecraft, Call of Duty, Fallout, Warcraft, Halo and Candy Crush. Current adaptations include Amazon's Fallout, a Diablo animated series and a Call of Duty film at Paramount.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A producer bringing Minecraft or Fallout to the screen now negotiates with an owner that runs its own merchandise, sponsorship and theme-park lines, which may make the producer's share of those lines the term that decides the deal.
The Facts
  • XP ("experience points") announced Oct. 8, 2026 by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma (memo on Xbox Wire); chief strategy officer Matthew Ball outlined the vision to staff.
  • Four units: XBOX PICTURES (film and TV adaptations), XBOX PRODUCTS (licensing and merchandise), XBOX PARTNERSHIPS (sponsors, brand partners), XBOX PLACES (broadcast and in-person events, theme parks, location-based experiences).
  • President: Kayleen Walters, previously president of Mojang; 13 years at Lucasfilm; grew Minecraft consumer products into "a multibillion-dollar business with more than 250 licensees"; executive producer of A Minecraft Movie (biggest U.S. film of 2025 per Sharma; top five worldwide) and a producer of the sequel. Mojang secured a deal for the first of several planned Minecraft theme parks under her.
  • Franchises named: Minecraft, Call of Duty, Fallout, Warcraft, Gears of War, Candy Crush, Diablo, Forza, The Elder Scrolls, Halo.
  • Existing and upcoming adaptations: A Minecraft Movie (Warner Bros.), Fallout (Amazon), Diablo animated series, Call of Duty film at Paramount, film and TV rights to Hideo Kojima's Physint.
  • Mojang successor: Maria Angelidou-Smith (ex-Meta, ex-Reddit chief product officer), starts Oct. 19.
  • Calendar context: A Minecraft Movie Squared is dated July 23, 2027 (Deadline, Warner Bros. slate list).

Skydance's Film Chiefs Now Decide Which Warner Bros. Projects Survive, Starting With Barbie 2
Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein inherit Warner's 2027 to 2029 slate, including an unsettled Barbie 2, Jonah Hill's finished but undated The Cut Off, and Baz Luhrmann's Jehanne d'Arc, awaiting a new draft.
Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, who took over Paramount Pictures 14 months ago, now also run Warner Bros.: nine film labels, three animation units and a commitment to more than 30 theatrical films a year. Deadline lists the Warner projects awaiting their review, from Barbie 2 to Jonah Hill's comedy The Cut Off, pulled from its date. New regimes have cut inherited work before: Warner shelved the completed Batgirl in 2022, and Paramount dropped Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Last Ronin in 2025. The Ankler reports co-CEO Ynon Kreiz is expected to oversee cost cuts.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Every Warner Bros. film approved under De Luca and Abdy is now Goldberg and Greenstein's to revisit, and the last two regime changes shelved finished films too, so the value sits in guaranteed pay and the right to take a dropped film elsewhere.
The Facts
  • Goldberg and Greenstein (Skydance Pictures co-chairs) take over the 2027-2029 Warner Bros. theatrical slates after Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy's exit.
  • Deadline's "first fire": ensuring Barbie 2 happens with Greta Gerwig, Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling (Barbie grossed $1.44 billion). The Cut Off (Jonah Hill directs and stars with Kristen Wiig) is reportedly finished and was undated after being set against The Odyssey.
  • Jehanne d'Arc (Baz Luhrmann): dated Nov. 22, 2028, awaiting next draft, hoping for a spring start. Gladys (Weapons prequel, New Line) dated Sept. 8, 2028, awaiting a final draft before attaching a director.
  • Precedents (Deadline): Batgirl shelved and Coyote vs. Acme written down and sold when De Luca and Abdy arrived in 2022; Paramount's R-rated TMNT: The Last Ronin did not move to a greenlight after Goldberg and Greenstein arrived in 2025.
  • Structure (The Ankler): nine labels (Warner Bros., Paramount, New Line, Primal, Clockwork, Republic, Paramount Animation, Warner Bros. Animation, Skydance Animation) plus DC under Gunn and Safran; New Line, Clockwork and the Warner Bros. brand confirmed to survive. A Warner Bros. insider predicts the three animation units will collapse into one pipeline.
  • Ynon Kreiz (co-CEO, Deadline): "The plan is to keep the studios independent creatively, so that each will have its own slate, its own relationship... and then we will choreograph the release schedule." Ellison: "One of the things I'm a big believer in is original storytelling."
  • Financial context: $79 billion net debt; pro forma content spend of $30 billion-plus a year. Deadline notes that paying the settlement's $30 million per undelivered film (the payment goes to the guilds' health and retirement plans, filed 9/30) is cheaper than risking a $300 million film.

Los Angeles Soundstages Now Sell at a Fraction of Their 2021 Prices
Netflix is closing in on Radford Studio Center at about a fifth of the nearly $2 billion Hackman Capital paid in 2021, and L.A. stage occupancy fell to 62 percent in 2025.
Hackman Capital Partners paid nearly $2 billion for Radford in 2021, defaulted this year on more than $1 billion of related debt, and lost the lot to a Goldman Sachs-led lender takeover. The Hollywood Reporter reports Netflix is closing in on Radford at about a fifth of that price, and four of Hackman's five major L.A. properties are for sale. Soundstage occupancy fell to 62 percent in 2025, the lowest FilmLA has recorded. Warner Bros. filled 91 percent of its Burbank lot by steering its own showrunners there.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Independent L.A. stages are repricing at a fraction of 2021 values while Warner Bros. filled 91 percent of its Burbank lot with its own shows, which may leave stage rates open to negotiation everywhere except on a studio's own lot.
The Facts
  • Radford Studio Center (Studio City): Hackman Capital paid nearly $2 billion in 2021, largely debt-financed; ViacomCBS sold it to Hackman and Square Mile Capital for $1.85 billion. Hackman defaulted earlier in 2026 on more than $1 billion of debt tied to the lot; a Goldman Sachs-led lender takeover followed.
  • Netflix is "closing in on a deal at about a fifth of that price" (THR).
  • Four of Hackman's five major L.A. studio properties are being shopped, including Television City. An unnamed source: "In L.A., I think it's a curtain call for Hackman."
  • Property tax appeals since 2020 by the companies controlling the major lots: 269 appeals, about $319 million clawed back in decided cases; Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, Universal and Sony account for more than $245 million.
  • Sony Pictures Studios (Culver City): county cut about $166.3 million, an 84 percent reduction on a $198 million assessment. WBD Burbank: argued $700 million should be as low as $212 million; county cut about $51.7 million. Universal asked in 2023 to cut its assessment from $951 million to $60 million. Paramount won about $15.6 million across 14 appeals.
  • FilmLA soundstage occupancy: 90 percent (2022), 69 percent (2023), 62 percent (2025, lowest recorded). Episodic TV was about a fifth of stage production in 2023, down from about 30 percent; scripted TV shoot days fell another 23 percent in 2024.
  • Warner Bros. lot occupancy last year: 91 percent. Simon Robinson, president of global experiences and studio operations: "We were at highs effectively for all of last year."
  • New supply: East End Studios' $230 million Mission Campus (January); Cinespace six-stage Woodland Hills facility (March); Echelon, $450 million, opening later this year; FilmLA tracks seven more planned builds or renovations.

Fox Nation's Houdini Series Puts AI Faces on Real Actors
Red Rock Films used AI-assisted motion capture to change the appearance of the actors playing Harry Houdini and his wife Bess, working from licensed archival footage and some 400 photographs.
Fox Nation premieres Houdini: Back From the Dead on Oct. 14, a three-part docuseries timed to the 100th anniversary of Houdini's death on Oct. 31. The streamer calls it its first long-form production "to rely entirely on AI-generated imagery." Red Rock Films, the Emmy-winning producer of Secrets of the Whales, altered the actors' appearance with AI-assisted motion capture, generated the re-enactments, and stages an AI Houdini interview built from his letters and diaries. People wrote the scripts. Red Rock says the process costs less than traditional CGI motion capture.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): On Houdini: Back From the Dead the actors supply the performances and the screen shows faces built from 400 licensed photographs, which may move the value toward the motion-capture and credit terms for a performance shown under another person's likeness.
The Facts
  • Title: Houdini: Back From the Dead, three parts, premieres Oct. 14, 2026 on Fox Nation; Houdini died Oct. 31, 1926.
  • Fox Nation: its first long-form production "to rely entirely on AI-generated imagery."
  • Producer: Red Rock Films (Secrets of the Whales, Penguin Town), which has an AI division.
  • Method: AI-assisted motion capture altered the appearance of the human actors playing Houdini, Bess and others; re-enactments and other visuals AI-generated; licensed archival footage and some 400 photographs as source material.
  • Scripts written by people, with "archival research and expert review."
  • An AI-generated Houdini sits for an interview, using words from his correspondence and diaries.
  • Red Rock: the AI-assisted motion capture process is less expensive and more efficient than traditional CGI mo-cap.
  • Lauren Petterson, president, Fox Nation: "Fox Nation is breaking new creative ground by using emerging technology to bring one of history's most fascinating figures to life for a modern audience."
